hero.bars_cap: The lots, by high estimate

changed.text: Bonhams brings more than three hundred jewels to the block in California on Tuesday, and the most telling lots are the smallest. Three unmounted fancy-color diamonds anchor the sale: a 1.01-carat oval fancy pink-purple estimated to about $50,000, a 1.64-carat fancy deep pink to roughly $35,000, and a 0.53-carat heart-shaped fancy blue also near $35,000.

means.who: Watch the no-reserve necklace as the sale's honest number.
means.text: Estimates are a house's opinion; a lot with no floor prints whatever the market truly thinks a 70-carat necklace is worth on a Tuesday in July — and that figure will say more about the mid-market than any record would.

visual.cap: Table I · The lots, by high estimate
visual.note: Upper estimates, USD thousands. Bonhams California, July 28. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/137

sections.h: The smallest lots say the most

p.text: In a category where top color can command seven figures, these are deliberately accessible numbers.

Above them sits the sale's marquee curiosity: a 70-carat diamond necklace of pear, oval and marquise stones carrying an upper estimate of just $50,000 — and offered with no reserve, meaning it will sell to the highest bid however low.

A 1920s necklace built around a 7.10-carat center stone is estimated near $35,000, and a multicolored sapphire-and-diamond necklace, 34.95 carats of sapphires to 4.20 of diamonds, at about $28,000. Van Cleef & Arpels, Graff and Boucheron appear throughout.

sections.h: A necklace with no floor

p.lead: The strategy is legible in the estimates.
p.text: No-reserve lots and conservative valuations are how a house generates competition and clears estate material in a cautious market: set the bar low, let the room find the price.

It is the opposite of the trophy-lot playbook that carried the spring's headline sales, and a useful barometer of where mid-market demand actually sits when the eight-figure stones are not in the room.

sections.h: Paying for the unmanufacturable

p.lead: It also reads against the week's other diamond story.
p.text: Natural stones are competing on rarity and provenance as lab-grown collapses the price of size; fancy color — genuinely scarce, impossible to grow to order at scale — is where that argument is strongest.
A room bidding up small pinks and blues is a room still paying for what cannot be manufactured.

hero.bars_cap: A giant and a newborn

changed.text: Qatar has opened its first diamond exchange, and its ambition is not subtle.

means.text: The Gulf is not short of diamond capacity, so Doha's real target is not Antwerp or Surat but the dealer deciding where to clear the next parcel. Qatar has built the room and written the rules; now it has to give the trade a reason to walk in rather than fly on to Dubai.

visual.cap: Table I · A giant and a newborn
visual.note: Annual diamond trade. Doha starts from zero. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/138

sections.h: A hub with ambition

p.text: The Qatar Free Zones Authority launched the Qatar Diamond Exchange this week at the Ras Bufontas free zone near Doha, describing it as a regulated hub that gathers the full diamond and precious-stones value chain within a single regulated ecosystem, in the words of chief executive Sheikh Mohammed Bin Hamad Bin Faisal Al-Thani.
Its natural rival sits an hour's flight away in Dubai.

p.lead: The plumbing is built for the trade's real needs.
p.text: Members — traders, manufacturers, cutters, polishers and service firms — get trading licences, on-site sorting and independent valuation, secure vaulting, specialist insurance, and the right to take part in rough and polished tenders.
Free-zone terms in Qatar typically allow full foreign ownership and favorable tax treatment, the incentives every aspiring hub uses to pull goods and dealers off established routes.

sections.h: The plumbing is real

p.lead: Qatar has been laying the groundwork quietly.
p.text: It joined the Kimberley Process as a full member in 2021 and, in 2025, designated the free-zone authority as the country's sole authorized entry and exit point for rough diamonds — the regulatory spine an exchange needs before it can credibly host tenders.
The launch turns that framework into a marketplace.

sections.h: Liquidity follows trust

p.lead: Whether it draws real liquidity is the harder question.
p.text: Dubai posted a record $41.7 billion in diamond trade in 2025 and has spent two decades building the relationships that route stones through it; Antwerp and Mumbai are older still.
A new exchange can offer better terms, but volume follows trust, and trust in this trade is measured in decades, not incentives.

hero.bars_cap: Burma ruby, regraded

changed.lead: When the reference book changes shape, the market has already moved.
changed.text: GemGuide, the pricing service the American colored-stone trade leans on, has revised its ruby charts: Mozambique prices raised sharply on strong demand for unenhanced, untreated material, and the Burma section rebuilt from the ground up.

means.text: Ruby is quietly running the colored-stone story diamonds used to own — a scarce natural material getting scarcer, priced by origin and honesty rather than size. When the guide stops grading a stone the old way, it is telling you the supply, not the demand, is the thing that broke.

visual.cap: Table I · Burma ruby, regraded
visual.note: The only four grades GemGuide now prices for unenhanced Burma ruby. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/139

sections.h: The book changes shape

p.text: Research director Stuart Robertson said Mozambique prices have, in effect, skyrocketed as tender buyers chase clean goods.

p.lead: The Burma change is the more striking admission.
p.text: GemGuide abandoned its traditional one-to-ten quality scale for unenhanced Burmese ruby and now publishes just four grades — Middle Commercial, Lower Good, Upper Fine and Upper Extra Fine — leaving users to interpolate the rest.
The reason is scarcity: fine Mogok material has become so hard to source that availability now matters more than price. You cannot chart a stone that does not come to market.

sections.h: Too scarce to grade

p.text: Mozambique has carried the category for over a decade, and its tenders — Gemfields' chief among them — now set the global reference for gem and near-gem ruby.

That is where the price pressure is coming from: a single dominant source, buyers competing for untreated goods, and a treatment-disclosure culture that has taught the trade to pay a real premium for stones that have not seen the furnace.

sections.h: Origin over size

p.text: The revisions go live in the service's app immediately and reach print in the July–August issue.

For appraisers and retailers that means the number under a ruby changed this week whether or not the stone did — the kind of quiet repricing that ripples through insurance values and estate valuations long after the tender room empties.

hero.bars_cap: India's June export tape

changed.lead: The Indian trade is voting with its badges.
changed.text: GJEPC's IIJS Premiere, the country's flagship gem-and-jewellery show, returns to Mumbai on August 6–10, and pre-registration has already crossed 25,000 with the first deadline extended to absorb demand.

means.who: Watch the order books, not the footfall.
means.text: Registrations measure hope; the tickets written between August 6 and 10, against a live US tariff and a soft rough market, will show whether India's recovery is broad enough to survive the loss of a little American duty-free room.

visual.cap: Table I · India's June export tape
visual.note: Year-on-year change, June 2026. GJEPC. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/140

sections.h: Voting with their badges

p.text: For a domestic industry that spent the spring absorbing tariff shocks, an early sell-out of visitor slots is its own kind of forecast.

p.lead: The confidence has a number behind it.
p.text: India's gross gems-and-jewellery exports rose 26.5 percent in June to about $2.21 billion, led by gold jewellery up 54.5 percent and cut-and-polished diamonds up 8.7 percent.
The quarter as a whole was flat, and rough imports fell by roughly a third, so the June jump is a restart rather than a boom — but a restart is what the show floor is built to convert into orders.

sections.h: A restart, not a boom

p.lead: The backdrop is anything but settled.
p.text: A new 10 percent US duty on Indian goods took effect on July 24, landing on the single largest market for Surat's polished output, and the European exemption for stones finished in Antwerp gives buyers a reason to route work away from India.
A strong domestic show is partly a hedge: if the American door narrows, the Indian counter and Gulf buyers have to carry more of the weight.

sections.h: A hedge against the duty

p.text: That is why GJEPC has spent the summer courting retailers well beyond Mumbai, from Lucknow to Abu Dhabi, ahead of the doors opening.
The show is no longer only an export shop window; it is where India's own fast-growing jewellery retail — the demand behind Titan's 39 percent quarter — meets its supply base under one roof.

hero.bars_cap: Israeli diamond exports · the long slide
hero.n: Nissim Zuaretz, president, after two years

changed.text: Nissim Zuaretz resigned as president of the Israel Diamond Exchange on July 26 after two years in the role, and the figure he left behind explained the exit more plainly than any statement could.

means.text: A bourse is only as strong as the reasons to trade inside it, and Ramat Gan is watching those reasons move to the Gulf one lease at a time. A record-low half is not a headline the next president inherits so much as a mandate, and the mandate is blunt: give the floor a reason to stay that is larger than a tax bill, or preside over the goodbye Zuaretz already named.

visual.cap: Table I · Israeli diamond exports · the long slide
visual.note: Polished diamond export value. Half-year 2026 vs. 2015 full-year peak. The floor that took a president with it. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/125

sections.h: A record-low half

p.text: Israeli diamond exports came to $2.4 billion in the first half of 2026, the lowest half on record and a fraction of the roughly $7 billion the country shipped at its 2015 peak. A trade that once ran through Ramat Gan is running somewhere else.

Zuaretz named the pressures without softening them: dealers and their goods relocating to Dubai for its tax treatment, lab-grown stones hollowing out the middle of the natural market, weakening global demand, and a new United States tariff on diamond imports that took effect over the weekend.

That measure is the Section 301 forced-labour tariff of 24 July, under which Israel sits in the 12.5% tier; the 10% Section 122 surcharge it replaced was sunsetting the same day. Without a change of course, he warned, "we will be able to say goodbye to the Israel Diamond Exchange."

sections.h: Where the trade went

p.lead: The exchange is not a small room.
p.text: Its four-tower complex in Ramat Gan has for decades been one of the world's principal trading floors, a place where memo goods and sight boxes changed hands under one roof.

The migration Zuaretz described is the quiet kind: not a closure but a slow draining of the firms, the workers and the inventory that gave the floor its liquidity, each one following a lower cost of doing business to the Gulf.

sections.h: The cut that compounds

p.lead: The tariff is the sharpest of the new cuts.
p.text: The 12.5% American duty, the upper of the two Section 301 bands that hit roughly sixty countries on July 24, lands on a trade already competing with a Dubai that charges little to nothing, and it compounds rather than replaces the structural drift.
An election to replace Zuaretz, already expected in November, now carries the weight of deciding whether the exchange fights the drift or manages the decline.

corrections: Correction, 25 August 2026: this article as published said that a new 10% United States tariff on diamond imports took effect over the weekend of 24 July, and repeated the 10% figure in its third paragraph and in the panel. The rate is wrong and the measure was conflated with the one it replaced. The 10% duty was the Section 122 general import surcharge, which was sunsetting on or about 24 July; what took effect that day was a new Section 301 forced-labour tariff covering 60 economies at 10% or 12.5%, and Israel sits in the 12.5% tier. The bad figure was this paper's own framing and not the trade press it drew on: Rapaport's report of the resignation, re-fetched today, carries no tariff percentage at all, and no percentage was attributed to Zuaretz. What was right as published: that a new American duty struck Israeli goods in late July, that it lands on a trade already losing firms to Dubai, and every export figure in the piece. This is the same fault corrected on this paper's 23 August Israel filing on 24 August; that run fixed the page it was pointed at and did not check the rest of the archive for the same sentence. Found here on 25 August by grepping every article for the figure, which is what should have happened the first time.

hero.bars_cap: Who has hardened the language
hero.src: On the record · the terminology turn

changed.lead: The word on the tag is about to change.
changed.text: CIBJO, the world jewelry confederation, expects to remove "laboratory-grown" and "laboratory-created" from its Blue Book and require the single term "synthetic" for man-made gemstones, with a formal decision due at its congress on September 4.

means.text: Language is the cheapest lever in this trade and the slowest to move, which is exactly why the naturals side is pulling it now. Call a stone synthetic often enough and the market stops arguing about whether it is a diamond, and that argument, not the carat price, is the one that has always been worth winning.

visual.cap: Table I · Who has hardened the language
visual.note: Bars mark relative reach of each rule, not a measured quantity. The dictionary as a price list. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/126

sections.h: One word, by decree

p.text: The body concluded the older phrasing described the product poorly, and that a plainer word serves the shopper better.

Charles Abouchar, who heads CIBJO's colored-stone commission, framed the aim as "protecting consumer confidence through the adoption of clear and descriptive language." The confederation's own definition does the heavy lifting: a synthetic is an artificial product with essentially the same chemical composition, physical properties and structure as its natural counterpart.
That is precisely the claim lab-grown marketers have leaned on, now recast in a word the trade has historically used to mean cheaper.

sections.h: A coordinated push

p.lead: CIBJO is not moving alone.
p.text: Russia ordered lab-grown jewelry labeled "synthetic" from September 1, the African Diamond Producers Association made the same call in May, India's Bureau of Indian Standards issued standardized terminology, and the GIA updated its own terms in 2025.

Read together, the moves are a natural-diamond counteroffensive fought on the dictionary rather than the price list, aimed at stripping the borrowed romance out of a category whose wholesale prices have fallen about 96% since 2018.

sections.h: What it costs the counter

p.lead: For retailers the change is not cosmetic.
p.text: A sales associate who has spent three years teaching customers to say "lab-grown" now has to unlearn it, and a word that markets a product as modern and guilt-free becomes a word that markets it as manufactured.
The stakes are largest for the brands that built their pitch on the friendlier phrase, and smallest for the naturals houses that lobbied for the harder one.

hero.bars_cap: June price move by size · smalls lead

changed.lead: The diamond recovery has a size, and the size is small.
changed.text: The RapNet Diamond Index for 0.30-carat stones rose 4.2% in June, accelerating from a 2.1% gain in May, and half-carat goods added 1.3%, while the one-carat index slipped 0.7% on the month. Three-carat stones edged back to positive at 0.4%.

means.text: When the thirty-pointer moves before the one-carat, it is telling you the recovery is being made in the back office, not the boutique. Watch the half-carat into IIJS, because if the smalls hold their gains through a restocked August, the middle of the book is next, and the middle is where the money is.

visual.cap: Table I · June price move by size · smalls lead
visual.note: RapNet Diamond Index, month-on-month, June 2026. Bars show size, not sign. The recovery starts small. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/127

sections.h: Small stones, real gains

p.text: The turn is genuine, but it is running from the bottom of the scale upward, not the top down.

p.lead: The engine is scarcity, not exuberance.
p.text: Sustained inventory reductions have let dealers correct small-stone prices upward, helped by steady United States retail demand through June and healthy Hong Kong counters at Chow Tai Fook and Luk Fook.

Indian wholesalers expect activity to firm further into the August IIJS Premiere show in Mumbai and the October wedding season, the two dates that usually decide whether a soft summer becomes a real fourth quarter.

sections.h: Scarcity, not exuberance

p.lead: Supply has been thinning at the source as well.
p.text: De Beers cut official rough prices sharply, particularly for goods under 0.75 carats, to meet the market it actually faces, and global rough production fell 8% to 98.8 million carats in 2025, with Russia leading by value for a third straight year.
Indian manufacturers, still cautious, have kept polishing lines deliberately short rather than betting on a broad rebound.

sections.h: The divergence to watch

p.lead: The divergence is the story worth watching.
p.text: Large stones, two carats and up in the better colors and clarities, remain the strongest sellers on the American counter, yet the price recovery is starting in the smalls, where tight inventory bites first.
A market that heals from both ends at once is rare, and this one is choosing the cheaper end to start.

hero.bars_cap: The levels that box gold in

changed.lead: Gold enters the most consequential week of its summer wound tight.
changed.text: Spot held the low $4,000s to start Monday, capped by resistance near $4,100 and floored by support at $4,022 and, below it, the triple-bottom zone around $3,964.

means.text: The triangle will not hold through three top-tier prints, so position for the break rather than the level. For the jewelry counter the number that matters is not the peak but the floor, and as long as $3,964 holds, gold stays the value story a nervous shopper is already buying.

visual.cap: Table I · The levels that box gold in
visual.note: USD/oz. Technical markers into the July 28–29 FOMC. A triangle waiting on the Fed. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/128

sections.h: Wound tight under $4,100

p.text: Chart readers call the shape a symmetrical triangle, the kind that resolves into a decisive move rather than a drift, and this week hands it three reasons to break.

p.lead: The calendar is dense.
p.text: The Federal Reserve announces its decision on July 28–29, with a hold at 3.50–3.75% widely expected but markets still pricing a small chance of a hike.

Second-quarter GDP lands the same week, with the Atlanta Fed's tracker near 1.7% growth, and core PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, is seen around 3.3% against a headline near 3.7%. Any one of the three can move the metal; the combination can set its direction into August.

sections.h: Three prints, one week

p.lead: The risk is in the tone, not the number.
p.text: A hold read as "higher for longer" would lift Treasury yields and press gold back under $4,100, while balanced language paired with softer yields would let bullion test the resistance and, beyond it, the $4,132 and $4,173 markers.
The white metals sit in the same current: silver held near $58 with $60 in view, and platinum steadied around $1,585 after a soft week.

sections.h: A patient physical bid

p.lead: Physical demand is doing the quiet work beneath the chart.
p.text: Central-bank appetite remains firm, and Asian buying has stayed heavy even as Western funds hesitate, a split that has kept the floor higher than the technicals alone would justify.
That is the tension into Wednesday: a nervous financial bid above ground, a patient physical bid beneath it, and a Fed that gets to decide which one sets the price.

changed.lead: China bought the dip in size.
changed.text: The country imported roughly 173 tonnes of gold in June, its heaviest monthly inflow since March 2024, carrying first-half imports toward 820 tonnes.

means.text: 173 tonnes in a month is not a headline, it is a foundation, and it is being poured while the West debates whether to buy at all. For the jewelry trade the read is simple: the world's largest gold-buying public treats every dip as a discount, and that habit is worth more to the price than any single Fed sentence.

sections.h: A 173-tonne month

p.text: The number matters because of its timing: it landed as gold pulled back from above $4,100 toward $4,000, the exact move that chills Western investors and warms Chinese buyers.

p.lead: The pattern is now familiar but no less telling.
p.text: When the price sags, the East restocks.

Chow Tai Fook reported weight-based gold jewelry up 63.7% in Hong Kong and Macau and 38% on the mainland last quarter as softer prices revived demand, and the import figure is the wholesale echo of that retail pull, metal moving toward the counters that sell it by the gram rather than the story.

sections.h: A split market

p.lead: It is a split market.
p.text: Western fund flows have wavered into the Federal Reserve's July 28–29 meeting, wary that a hawkish hold lifts yields and dulls a metal that pays no interest.

Chinese demand runs on the opposite logic: a lower dollar price is a buying signal, not a warning, and central-bank and household appetite has kept building through the very weakness that unsettles the paper market.

sections.h: The floor it builds

p.lead: The consequence shows up as a floor.
p.text: Heavy physical offtake in the East is a large part of why gold has held the low $4,000s rather than retracing further, cushioning the pullbacks that the charts keep threatening.
The question into Wednesday is whether Fed messaging can pull Western money back to the same side of the trade the East has never left.

hero.bars_cap: Above retail, below retail · the resale board

changed.lead: The secondary market recovered in the second quarter, and it recovered unevenly.
changed.text: Morgan Stanley's latest read, built on WatchCharts data snapshotted June 29, puts value retention, the gap between retail and resale, at 15.4% above list for Patek Philippe, 9.8% for Rolex and 3.0% for Audemars Piguet.

means.text: Value retention is a popularity contest with a price attached, and the big three keep winning it by making less than the market wants. For anyone buying to hold, the lesson is unromantic: the badge and the reference matter more than the movement, and the resale board has been saying so for three straight quarters.

visual.note: Value retention vs. retail, Q2 2026 (Morgan Stanley × WatchCharts). Bars show size, not sign. Three names hold the line. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/130

sections.h: Three names, everyone else

p.text: Every other brand the bank tracks trades below retail, with Cartier at −27.4%, Omega at −32.3% and IWC at −37.9%.

p.lead: The gap is widening, not closing.
p.text: Patek's retention improved by more than ten points year on year and Rolex's by seven, so the recovery that lifted the market as a whole lifted the top three fastest.
The bank's own verdict was cool on everyone else: gains for the listed players remain modest, and the numbers still suggest limited pricing power outside the big three in the coming quarters.

sections.h: The gap is widening

p.lead: Underneath the brand averages, the models tell a sharper story.
p.text: Patek's Aquanaut trades about 90% above retail and the Nautilus 74% above, while the dressier Calatrava sits 34% below. Rolex's Oyster Perpetual runs 35% over list and the Sea-Dweller 21% under.
The premium is not to a maker so much as to a specific steel sports reference the waiting list never satisfied.

sections.h: A barbell for buyers

p.lead: For retailers and collectors the signal is a barbell.
p.text: The pieces that hold or gain are a narrow band of hyped sports models from three houses; almost everything else, including some very good watchmaking, is a depreciating asset the moment it leaves the boutique.
A recovery that concentrates this hard is really a flight to the same handful of names buyers already trusted.

changed.lead: The arithmetic is the hook.
changed.text: When Bonhams sells its California Jewels auction in Los Angeles on July 28, the marquee lot is a 70-carat diamond necklace of pear, oval and marquise stones estimated at up to $50,000, and offered without reserve.

means.text: A 70-carat necklace with no reserve is a dare disguised as a lot, and someone will take it. Watch the hammer against the low estimates rather than the highs, because in a no-reserve room the honest signal is not what the trophy makes but what the ordinary lots hold.

sections.h: The dare in the catalogue

p.text: Seventy carats of graded diamond for the price of a single fine solitaire is not a market on the diamonds; it is a market on the setting, the certification and the story.

p.lead: That is the estate logic of a no-reserve sale.
p.text: Older mounted pieces, whose individual stones are hard to certify and expensive to break out, trade at a steep discount to the loose-goods price sheet, and a seller who wants a clean, guaranteed sale accepts it.
The estimate is a floor to walk in the door, not a valuation of the carats, and the room, not the book, sets the price.

sections.h: Estate logic

p.text: The catalogue runs deeper than one lot.

Bonhams lists more than 300 jewels including a 1920s necklace built around a 7.10-carat diamond at a $35,000 high estimate, a necklace set with 34.95 carats of multicolored sapphires and 4.20 carats of diamonds at $28,000, and three unmounted diamonds estimated between $35,000 and $50,000, with signed pieces from Van Cleef & Arpels, Graff and Boucheron threaded through the sale.

sections.h: What the day sale measures

p.text: The venue is the point as much as the goods.

A California day sale is where the accessible middle of the jewelry market clears, the estate and secondary material that never reaches a Geneva evening, and it is a fair gauge of what ordinary collectors will pay in a summer when the metal underneath every lot has rarely been dearer.

cells.label: The change

hero.bars_cap: How common is fluorescence
hero.src: On the record · the report change

changed.text: One of the most persistent discounts in diamonds is about to get a footnote. From the fourth quarter of 2026, the GIA will add clarifying language to its grading reports to distinguish when fluorescence changes a diamond's appearance from when it does not.

means.text: This is a rare case of a grading change that helps the buyer and the seller at once, by pricing a stone for what it looks like instead of what it might do. Read the new line when it lands, because a diamond that glows and shows nothing for it may be the best-value stone in the case.

visual.cap: Table I · How common is fluorescence
visual.note: Share of diamonds exhibiting fluorescence, per GIA. Midpoint shown. A quarter of the case, finally explained. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/132

sections.h: A footnote on a discount

p.text: The trade has called it one of the biggest steps a laboratory has taken to address a trait that between 25% and 35% of diamonds carry to some degree.
Fluorescence, the soft glow some diamonds give under ultraviolet light, has been priced as a defect for decades even though it rarely is one.
In most stones it does nothing visible; in a small share it can lend a milky or oily cast to high-color goods, and the market long ago collapsed those two very different cases into a single penalty.
Rapaport has published fluorescence discount estimates since 1993, tracking a haircut that persisted through every swing of the market.

sections.h: Priced as a defect

p.lead: The fix is information, not chemistry.
p.text: By stating on the report whether the fluorescence actually affects the look of the specific stone, the GIA lets a buyer separate the harmless from the compromised, and lets a seller defend a price rather than accept a reflex discount.
For a sizable, long-misunderstood slice of the market, transparency about the trait could carry real weight with the trade and the shopper alike.

sections.h: Information, not chemistry

p.lead: The commercial stakes sit with the middle of the counter.
p.text: Faint and medium fluorescence in the near-colorless grades is exactly the material a value-minded consumer buys, and a clearer report gives the honest retailer a tool to reclaim margin that the blanket stigma has been quietly bleeding away.

hero.bars_cap: Where the half's growth sat · by category signal

changed.text: American jewelry sales grew through the first half of 2026, but the growth was priced, not counted. Retail revenue rose 8.6% over the six months and 13% year on year in June, according to point-of-sale figures compiled by Tenoris, while the average purchase price climbed roughly 19% for the half and 20% in June.

means.text: Nine percent is a headline a jeweler can live with, but the honest number underneath it is the one on the tag, not the till. Sell the bracelet and the strand of pearls while the appetite for a real purchase is there, because a market held up by price is only ever one nervous quarter from finding out how many buyers it actually has.

visual.cap: Table I · Where the half's growth sat · by category signal
visual.note: US point-of-sale, H1 2026 (Tenoris). Bars show size, not sign. The half the ticket carried. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/118

sections.h: Bigger tickets, a thinner crowd

p.text: The store is ringing up bigger tickets from a thinner crowd, a pattern that flatters the top line and hides a narrowing base.

p.lead: The gain concentrated at the higher-priced end.
p.text: Bracelets, tennis styles in particular, led with a 14% revenue increase and double-digit growth in what shoppers were willing to spend on them. Pearl jewelry had what analysts called a surprisingly strong first half. Pendants and earrings held their own but trailed the leaders.
The through-line is that the pieces carrying the market are the ones with a higher entry price, not the impulse buys near the register.

sections.h: Two diamonds, two engines

p.lead: The two diamond categories tell different stories.
p.text: Natural-diamond jewelry grew revenue at a single-digit rate, with unit sales down but higher average selling prices making up the difference and gross margins holding firm. Lab-grown moved the opposite way: revenue rose almost entirely on more units sold, while the average amount spent stayed essentially flat.
One engine runs on price discipline, the other on volume, and rising rough costs could yet press on the cheaper of the two.

sections.h: Jewelry outran the mall

p.lead: Set against the wider economy, jewelry outran the mall.
p.text: US retail sales overall rose just 0.2% in June as tax-refund tailwinds faded and shoppers turned cautious.

Against that backdrop a double-digit jewelry month looks strong, but the composition matters: a market that grows by selling dearer goods to fewer hands rewards the specialist counter and squeezes the value end, where a shopper who used to trade up now often trades out.

changed.text: Chow Tai Fook, Greater China's largest jewelry chain, reported retail sales value up 15.1% year on year for the quarter to June, its fiscal first quarter. Mainland China supplied 83.6% of the total and grew 10.7%; Hong Kong, Macau and other markets, a sixth of the business, jumped 44.8%.

means.text: A 64% surge in gold jewelry is a metal story wearing a retail costume, and metal stories turn. The chains booking these numbers are selling grams while gold sits just off a record; the test is whether the same shoppers come back for a diamond or a design once the bullion trade cools, or whether the counter has simply become a savings account with a clasp.

visual.cap: Table I · Same-store gold vs design · Chow Tai Fook, quarter to June
visual.note: Same-store sales, quarter to June 2026 (company). Bars show size, not sign. Grams beat design when gold is cheap. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/119

sections.h: Fifteen up, and it isn't design

p.text: On a same-store basis the mainland's self-operated shops rose 19.6% and franchises 15.7%, while Hong Kong and Macau together climbed 41.7%, Hong Kong up 35% and Macau up 64.6%.

p.lead: One product line did the work.
p.text: Weight-based gold jewelry, sold by the gram rather than by design, saw same-store sales leap 38% in the mainland and 63.7% in Hong Kong and Macau, as a softer gold price after June's pullback pulled buyers back to the counter.
Fixed-price, design-led jewelry told the opposite story, slipping about 1% in the mainland. When gold reads as value, shoppers buy the metal and skip the markup.

sections.h: The whole region, one trade

p.lead: The pattern is regional, not a single company's.
p.text: Luk Fook posted quarterly retail sales up 32% and Chow Sang Sang up 16% over the same window, according to Rapaport's trade wire.

Across the big Hong Kong-listed names, the story is the same: gold-as-savings is doing the selling, and the strength runs deepest where local buyers treat a chain necklace as a store of wealth rather than an accessory.

sections.h: Rising sales, fewer doors

p.lead: Yet the footprint is shrinking even as sales rise.
p.text: Chow Tai Fook closed a net 258 mainland locations in the quarter, ending June with 5,434 points of sale, part of a multi-year rationalization of a once-sprawling network.

Its April-launched Dawn Collection cleared more than HK$870 million, and the group leaned on brand upgrades to lift average prices. Investors stayed cool: the shares traded down about 2% and are off roughly 13% over six months.

hero.bars_cap: The gold-silver ratio, tightening · index points

changed.lead: Silver did the moving as the week closed.
changed.text: The white metal rose about 2% on Friday to roughly $58 an ounce while gold sat little changed near $4,061, tightening the gold-silver ratio to about 69.5 from 70.7 at midweek.

means.text: A compressing ratio in a parked market is the sound of money looking for the exit that still moves. For the counter it barely registers, because a chain sold by the gram tracks gold, not silver, but for anyone trading the metals into Wednesday the signal is the same one it has been all month, that the next real move is the Fed's to give.

visual.cap: Table I · The gold-silver ratio, tightening · index points
visual.note: Gold-silver ratio, 23–24 Jul 2026 (USAGOLD). Lower = silver gaining. Silver closing the gap. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/120

sections.h: Silver keeps the bid

p.text: It is a small compression, but a telling one: when both metals stall, the one that keeps a bid is usually the one carrying an industrial story as well as a monetary one.

p.lead: Everything now waits on Washington.
p.text: The Federal Reserve meets July 28 and 29, and a hold is widely expected; futures put the odds of a hike next week near a third and closer to four-in-five by September. Gold has largely priced the pause, which is why the tape has gone quiet.
The move, when it comes, will be about tone rather than the decision itself, and a hawkish surprise would give the metal a reason to slip toward $4,000.

sections.h: The tape waits on the room

p.lead: The cross-currents are unusually loud for a quiet tape.
p.text: Crude has pushed to six-week highs on renewed US strikes on Iran and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, lifting inflation expectations, and two-year Treasury yields have reached a seventeen-month high.

Higher yields raise the cost of holding metal that pays no coupon, a headwind for gold, yet coin and bar premiums are holding firm as physical buyers treat anything under $4,100 as a level to accumulate rather than a top to sell.

sections.h: Why the cheaper metal leads

p.lead: Silver's edge in that standoff is its second job.
p.text: Roughly half its demand is industrial, from solar cells to electronics, and that leg draws incremental buying when the rate path is uncertain and the monetary trade is stuck.
A ratio near 69 is still historically wide, which is the bullish case the silver desk keeps making: if gold cannot break higher, the cheaper metal has the room to close the gap.

changed.lead: The diamond trade is thinning into its summer lull, but not evenly.
changed.text: Rapaport's trade wire reports Antwerp running short of goods, a shortage that is pushing buyers toward India even as the calendar empties out.

means.text: A shortage in one hub and a tax on another is the market telling cutters to pick a lane before the show opens. India has the goods the recovery wants and the tariff it does not, and the winners in Mumbai will be the houses that already know which stones go to New York through Antwerp and which stay home for everyone else.

visual.note: RapNet Diamond Index, to 23 Jul 2026 (Rapaport). Bars show size, not sign. The bottom of the range firms first. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/121

sections.h: One hub empties, another fills

p.text: US wholesale is described as steady despite the seasonal slowdown, and the hubs that normally cycle stock among themselves are instead watching demand drift east to the source.

Underneath the quiet is a recovery that has legs at the small end. The RapNet Diamond Index for 0.30-carat goods rose 0.79% on the week and 4.25% over the month, while one-carat commercial stones firmed and the benchmark one-carat category slipped a marginal 0.11% on the week.
Small and commercial goods are leading the turn again, the same shape the market showed in the spring, and that is precisely the segment India cuts best.

sections.h: Mumbai reads an opening

p.text: India is reading the moment as an opening.

The trade heads into IIJS Premiere in Mumbai, which opens August 6 and runs to the tenth, with unusual optimism for a summer show, and a goods shortage in Antwerp only sharpens the pull toward a country that polishes roughly nine in ten of the world's diamonds by piece.
If the recovery is real, the August floor in Mumbai is where it gets confirmed or denied.

sections.h: The tariff picks the lane

p.lead: The complication arrived last week in Washington.
p.text: A new 10% US Section 301 duty on Indian goods went live July 24, landing on the exact trade now flowing India's way, while diamonds polished in the European Union keep their exemption, a quiet incentive to route US-bound finishing back through Antwerp.
So the trade walks into August holding two things at once, a genuine recovery in the goods India makes and a fresh tax on selling them to its largest customer.

changed.lead: A mine that stopped digging is still producing diamonds.
changed.text: Rio Tinto recovered 33,000 carats from Diavik's remaining ore in the second quarter, months after the flagship Canadian operation closed in March, working through residual and stockpiled material rather than mining anything new.

means.text: The interesting number is not the 33,000 carats but the zero that follows them. sections.h: A dark mine still gives

p.text: It is a coda, not a comeback, but it is a reminder that a diamond mine does not go dark the day the last truck leaves the pit.

p.lead: The scale of the wind-down is stark in the numbers.
p.text: Second-quarter diamond output plunged 97% both from the prior quarter and year on year, and first-half production came to 1.1 million carats, down 51% from the same period in 2025.
Those are the arithmetic of closure: once the ore body is exhausted, volume collapses to whatever the plant can still recover from what remains above ground.

sections.h: The exit is complete

p.text: Diavik was Rio Tinto's last diamond asset, and its closure completes a deliberate exit from the business. The major shut the famous pink-producing Argyle mine in Western Australia in 2020 and walked away from the Fort a la Corne project in Canada in 2023, choosing to concentrate on metals and minerals.
Rio has said it will continue to manufacture and sell its final diamond production at least through the end of 2026.

sections.h: Scarcity gets the last word

p.lead: The timing gives those last carats an odd tailwind.
p.text: Certified Canadian goods carry a provenance premium, and they enter a market where a 50% US tariff now sits on Canadian goods and the natural-diamond scarcity argument is building on the back of mine closures worldwide.
The final run from a marquee Canadian mine reaches buyers who are short of exactly that story, even as the tariff complicates the route to the largest market for it.

sections.h: A name and a deadline

p.text: It is the clearest signal yet that the separation Anglo set in motion last year will actually close, and close this year.

p.lead: The house being sold is priced at a cyclical low.
p.text: De Beers reported an estimated first-half loss, with second-quarter rough sales down 44% year on year to $665 million and the average realized price down 32% to $105 a carat, even as production rose 88% in the quarter to leave first-half output up 46%.
More stones for far less money is the shape of a market where rough sells about a third below where it stood a year ago.

sections.h: Cutting supply to fit

p.lead: Supply is being trimmed to fit.
p.text: De Beers is planning a two-year production pause at Venetia, its flagship South African mine, a decision that pulls future carats out of a market already carrying too many.
For a buyer, that is both the risk and the logic of the deal: take control at the bottom, when the seller is cutting output because prices will not carry it.

sections.h: The wager on the cycle

p.lead: The stakes run beyond one transaction.
p.text: The Penny consortium would inherit a brand still synonymous with natural diamonds at the moment lab-grown stones have hollowed out the low end and fresh US tariffs cross the trade routes.
A year-end close would end Anglo's long diamond era and hand the industry's most storied name to owners betting that scarcity, not marketing, is what turns the cycle back up.

changed.text: While bullion writes the headlines and gold jewelry drives counters from Mumbai to Hong Kong, the color side of the trade is quietly sorting itself into winners and casualties.

means.text: Pearls and fine color are not losing to gold so much as being asked to prove they are not gold, and the good ones can. Sell the strand and the signed piece on rarity and hand, not on carat weight, because the shopper who wants value already bought the chain, and the one standing at the color case is there for something the metal counter cannot sell them.

visual.note: Same-store sales, quarter to June 2026 (company). Bars show size, not sign. When metal wins, design must argue. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/124

sections.h: Pearls hold their own

p.text: In the United States, pearl jewelry posted what analysts called a surprisingly strong first half, one of the standout categories in a market that grew 8.6% overall. Pearls, priced on nacre, luster and match rather than on metal weight, held their own in a year when weight was everything.

p.lead: The other end of the color trade gave ground.
p.text: In mainland China, Chow Tai Fook's fixed-price jewelry, the design-led, gem-set pieces that carry a maker's markup, slipped about 1% on a same-store basis in the quarter to June, even as the chain's weight-based gold jewelry leapt 38%.
When a gold chain reads as savings, a gem-set pendant has to justify itself on feeling, not value, and this year feeling lost the argument at the Chinese counter.

sections.h: The middle gives way

p.lead: The split is really one question asked twice.
p.text: When gold is cheap enough to buy as a store of wealth, design and color compete on emotion alone, and the categories that win are the ones with their own scarcity to sell.

Tennis bracelets, up 14% in the US, show that diamonds still move when the format is right; pearls show that a stone with no substitute keeps its lane. The losers are the middle pieces bought as gifts and priced as commodities.

sections.h: Sell the thing gold is not

p.lead: That is the argument high summer usually settles.
p.text: The season's high-jewellery launches lean hard on craft, heritage and rare stones precisely because those are the things a gram of gold cannot offer, and in a year of record metal the maisons selling rarity have the cleaner story.
The color desk that thrives now is the one that stops competing with bullion on price and starts competing with it on the one thing gold does not have, which is a face.

hero.bars_cap: Where the wall stands · indicative rate by center

changed.text: The Trump administration reset its tariff machinery on July 24, imposing fresh duties on imported jewelry, diamonds, gemstones and precious metals from roughly sixty countries.

means.who: A 10% floor is survivable; the uncertainty around it is not.
means.text: The EU carve-out is the tell, quietly steering polished volume toward Antwerp and away from Surat, and the promise of further inquiries means no importer can price a spring order with confidence.
Expect the near-term response to be the oldest one in the book: pull inventory forward, sit on the goods in transit, and pass what cannot be absorbed to the counter.

visual.cap: Table I · Where the wall stands · indicative rate by center
visual.note: *Canada's 50% country measure stacks separately. Section 301 bands, 24 Jul 2026. The two-band tariff wall on jewelry imports. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/111

sections.h: A new legal footing, an old kind of wall

p.text: The legal footing is new: with earlier levies struck down when the Supreme Court invalidated the administration's use of emergency economic powers, the White House reached instead for Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, framing the action as a response to countries said to under-enforce prohibitions on forced labor.
The practical effect is a two-band wall across the trade's supply map.

The higher band, 12.5%, falls on China, Hong Kong, Israel, Thailand, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates, the cutting floors, manufacturing centers and trading hubs that move a large share of the world's finished goods.

The 10% band covers a longer list that includes India, Canada, Mexico, Indonesia, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the United Kingdom. For a business that sources across a dozen borders before a stone reaches a display case, almost every common route now carries a number it did not carry a week ago.

sections.h: The exemptions are the whole game

p.lead: The exemptions are where the detail lives.
p.text: Diamonds and gemstones polished in the European Union keep the exemption they already held, an advantage that quietly rewards Antwerp and Idar-Oberstein against Surat and Bangkok.

The EU and Taiwan face a net-of-most-favored-nation approach that tops combined rates up to a 10% floor; Japan, South Korea and Switzerland are handled the same way under a 12.5% cap. Goods already in transit on July 24 are spared, a narrow window that importers spent the week trying to widen.

sections.h: The trade reads it as a beginning

p.text: The trade's compliance voices read the move as a beginning rather than an end. "The story is not over; people need to continue to pay attention," said Sara Yood of the Jewelers Vigilance Committee, noting that additional Section 301 inquiries into manufacturing capacity could add further duties later.

The new bands also stack onto country-specific measures already in force, including the 50% rate on Canadian goods and the separate action against Brazil, so a single shipment can now carry more than one layer.

hero.bars_cap: The seam · duty by finishing center

changed.text: No country has more exposed to the new tariff schedule than India, which cuts and polishes somewhere around ninety percent of the world's diamonds by piece count and sends a large slice of that output to American buyers.

means.text: The tariff does not fall on India so much as on the seam between India and America, and seams are where trades tear. A 10% wall around the cheapest labor in the pipeline invites the goods to route around it, and the EU carve-out draws the map.
For Surat, the danger is not this quarter's duty but the precedent that finishing a stone at home has become the expensive option.

visual.cap: Table I · The seam · duty by finishing center
visual.note: Same rough, different finish, different border. Section 301, 24 Jul 2026. Why the wall points away from Surat. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/112

sections.h: The busiest lane takes the hit

p.text: The 10% duty that took effect on July 24 is not the highest rate on the board, but it lands on the single busiest lane in the polished trade, and it lands at a moment when the men who own the wheels in Surat have the least room to give.

p.lead: That thin room is the second story inside the first.
p.text: Rough is cheap, with De Beers' realised price down about a third year on year, but cheap rough has not rescued cutters, because polished prices have fallen alongside it and the spread that pays a factory's wages has stayed narrow.

Surat spent the past year trimming shifts and idling benches; a fresh 10% at the border is a cost that has to be split three ways, among the exporter who books the sale, the American importer who takes the goods, and the shopper who eventually pays the ticket.

sections.h: The exemption draws a map around India

p.lead: The exemption for European-polished stones sharpens the choice.
p.text: A diamond that leaves India as rough, travels to Antwerp to be polished and enters the United States as EU goods can, on paper, sidestep the duty that the same stone would carry if finished in Gujarat.

Re-routing at scale is neither quick nor free, and rules of origin will be argued over for months, but the incentive now points away from the world's largest cutting center, which is precisely the outcome its exporters feared.

sections.h: Someone along the chain holds the difference

p.text: India's trade bodies have spent the season lobbying against exactly this, arguing that duties on polished goods punish a labor-intensive industry that competes on cost. The near-term arithmetic is unforgiving: at a 10% rate on a category already running on single-digit margins, some orders simply do not clear, and the ones that do move slower.
The question the trade will spend August answering is who, along that chain from bench to counter, is left holding the difference.

means.text: This is a coiled-spring week, and the spring is wound by Wednesday's statement, not by the tape itself. Gold at $4,061 is neither cheap nor frightened; it is parked.

sections.h: A market parked, not frightened

p.text: The metal is holding a high plateau rather than breaking out, which is the posture of a market waiting for someone else to move first. This week, that someone is the Federal Reserve.
The policy committee meets July 28 and 29, and the consensus expects it to leave rates where they are, echoing the European Central Bank's hold on Thursday.
The case for standing still got firmer late in the week when jobless claims came in at 187,000 against a forecast of 212,000, a labor market stronger than the models penciled in.
A stronger jobs picture cuts both ways for gold: it eases recession fear, but it keeps alive the prospect of higher rates later in the year if inflation stays above target.

sections.h: The whole game is the rate

p.lead: That rate-and-gold relationship is the whole game at these levels.
p.text: Higher interest rates raise the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no coupon, so a hawkish surprise on Wednesday would give the metal a reason to slip back toward $4,000, while any dovish tilt would hand it the excuse to test $4,100 again.
The white metals told their own story on Friday: silver added about 1.2% to $58.22, while platinum slipped 1.1% to $1,574.

sections.h: The bench prices a floor and a ceiling

p.text: For the jewelry trade, the number that matters is less the daily print than the shelf it sits on. Gold has spent July defending $4,000 rather than charging past it, and a market that merely holds a record is easier to design around than one that lurches.
Manufacturers pricing autumn collections are treating $4,000 as the floor and $4,100 as the ceiling until the Fed says otherwise.

hero.bars_cap: Platinum demand · thousand ounces, 2026 f'cast

changed.text: Platinum is that rare thing in commodities, a metal the world keeps running short of while its price refuses to celebrate.

means.text: Platinum's shortage is a supply story wearing a demand problem, and markets pay for the problem before they pay for the story. Four straight deficits should have lit a fire under the price; instead the metal sits at $1,574 because the buyers who would bid it up, jewelers and carmakers, are both stepping back.
The investment thesis is sound and early, which on a trading desk is another word for wrong, until it isn't.

visual.cap: Table I · Platinum demand · thousand ounces, 2026 f'cast
visual.note: WPIC 2026 forecast, thousand ounces. Deficit 297koz. A market undersupplied on paper. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/114

sections.h: Short on paper, soft on the screen

p.text: The World Platinum Investment Council now forecasts a 297,000-ounce deficit for 2026, the fourth consecutive year in which supply falls short of demand, and yet spot platinum slipped about 1% on Friday to $1,574 an ounce. Scarcity on paper and softness on the screen are, for now, coexisting.

p.lead: The demand mix explains the tension.
p.text: Total platinum demand is set to fall about 9% to 7,674,000 ounces, dragged by a 12% drop in jewelry use and a 2% dip in automotive, where the metal's traditional home in catalytic converters keeps shrinking.

What holds the market in deficit is elsewhere: industrial demand climbs 9% to 2,238,000 ounces on new glass-making capacity, and bar-and-coin investment jumps 27% to 718,000 ounces as buyers treat platinum as the cheap cousin of gold.

sections.h: Supply barely moves; stocks thin

p.lead: Supply, meanwhile, is barely moving.
p.text: Mine output is projected flat while recycling grows about 9%, lifting total supply only 2% and leaving the shortfall to be filled from above-ground stocks that the council expects to cover less than three months of global demand by the end of the year.
"The market continues to be undersupplied, and platinum demand is well insulated," said the council's chief executive, Trevor Raymond, pressing the investment case that price alone has yet to make.

sections.h: A demand problem wearing a supply story

p.text: For the jewelry bench, the 12% fall in platinum demand is the line that stings, and it is a demand problem, not a supply one.

High gold has not sent buyers to platinum in the numbers the metal's backers hoped; instead it has thinned the whole precious-jewelry category, and platinum, always the connoisseur's choice, feels it first. The deficit is real, but a deficit driven by collapsing jewelry offtake is a strange kind of bull case.

hero.bars_cap: How the counter was funded · share of jewelry sales

changed.lead: When the gold price finally blinked, India bought.
changed.text: The World Gold Council's July read on the market records a roughly 10% fall in the domestic price during June, to about 141,000 rupees per 10 grams, its lowest in six months, tracking an 11% slide in the international price to near $4,000.

means.text: This is a recycling recovery, not a demand boom, and the two are easy to confuse on a quarterly slide. When more than half of what crosses the counter is yesterday's gold coming back, revenue can grow while fresh appetite stays flat, and imports can fall while shops look busy.
India will buy every dip in gold; the open question is whether it will still buy the metal at a new high, or only the story of a bargain.

visual.note: WGC July 2026 read on India, Apr–Jun quarter. More than half the counter ran on yesterday's gold. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/115

sections.h: When the price blinked, India bought

p.text: Overall consumer demand stayed subdued, the council notes, but the drop was enough to pull jewelry buyers off the sidelines they had occupied through the spring's records.

p.lead: The listed chains felt it first.
p.text: Major organized jewellers reported revenue growth of 30% to 60% year on year for the April-to-June quarter, a number that looks heroic until the composition is examined.

As much as 43% to 55% of jewelry sales were funded not by fresh money but by old gold traded back across the counter, with exchange volumes rising a further 10% to 20% after a duty change nudged households to recycle rather than import.

sections.h: Screens take share from the safe at home

p.lead: Investment demand told a divided story.
p.text: Gold exchange-traded funds took in 34.4 billion rupees of net inflows in June, the most since February, lifting holdings 2.2 tonnes to 119 tonnes, and digital-gold transaction values rose to 25.5 billion rupees.
Bars and coins, the traditional hoard, cooled at the same time, a sign that the newer, screen-based ways of owning gold are quietly taking share from the safe at home.

sections.h: The froth comes off the import bill

p.lead: The import line shows how much the froth has come off.
p.text: June gold imports fell 42% from May to $1.97 billion, with volume down to somewhere between 16 and 22 tonnes from 29 tonnes, and gold's share of the country's merchandise import bill dropped to 3% from 17% in January.
The domestic market even swung to a discount averaging about $20 an ounce in early July, a world away from the $150 premium of May.

changed.lead: Two lines that used to move together are now moving apart.
changed.text: Swiss brands opened 2026 with US retail increases of about 7%, led by Rolex, Tudor and Audemars Piguet, while the secondary market spent the year sliding, with index trackers putting the broad decline near 8% and both Rolex and Patek Philippe touching two-year lows.

means.text: The era of the watch as a liquid asset is closing, and the counter should be glad of it. When the flip stops paying, the buyer who remains is the one who wanted the object rather than the arbitrage, and that is a healthier customer to build a business on.
The brands raising list prices into a falling secondary market are betting that desire outlives speculation. On the evidence of the rarest Pateks, they may be right.

sections.h: Two lines that used to move together

p.text: The list price went up; the street price went down; the gap between them is the whole subject.

p.lead: That gap is where the last cycle's speculation lived.
p.text: At the 2022 peak, a steel sports Rolex or a Nautilus traded far above its boutique price, and the premium was the reason people queued for waitlists they never intended to wear.

As the secondary market has cooled through 2026, that premium has compressed toward zero and, on many references, below it, which turns a flip into a loss and a waitlist into a formality rather than a lottery ticket.

sections.h: The market sorts the rare from the merely wanted

p.lead: The decline is not uniform, and the exceptions are instructive.
p.text: Rolex's secondary prices have held comparatively steady, the blue-chip behaving like a blue-chip, while Patek Philippe's broader range has been the weaker performer even as its scarcest complications keep setting gains.
The market, in other words, is sorting: the truly rare still appreciates, the merely desirable is repricing toward what a watch is actually worth to someone who wants to own it.

sections.h: A mixed blessing at the counter

p.lead: For retailers, the narrowing gap is a mixed blessing.
p.text: A secondary market that no longer trades at a fat premium removes the grey-market temptation that pulled buyers away from authorized doors, but it also strips the resale-value story that justified the primary purchase.
Selling a $15,000 sports watch is harder when last year's model can be had for less than list on a screen, and the January price increase only widens that spread.

sections.h: Marquetry meets the most geometric decade

p.text: Her new Art Deco collection, drawn up around the centenary of the 1925 Paris Exposition that gave the style its name, reads the 1920s not through diamonds and platinum but through texture, arranging chevrons, mosaics and spirals in materials most fine jewelers never touch.

p.lead: The material list is the statement.
p.text: Straw marquetry, the enchapado de tamo that is the house signature, sits alongside Japanese Shibayama inlay, mother-of-pearl and abalone, iridescent beetle-wing, black palm wood, coral and mirrored surfaces.

Egyptomania and Japonisme, the two exotic currents that fed original Deco, return here as surface and pattern rather than as motif, filtered through the hands of Brazilian and Asian artisans the studio has spent years training.

sections.h: An argument about where value sits

p.text: It is a deliberate argument about where value sits.

In a season when the natural-diamond price is falling and the lab-grown stone has made carat weight cheap, a collection that asks to be judged on the difficulty of its making rather than the size of its stones is making a case for craft as the last defensible luxury.
The pieces debuted at Couture in Las Vegas in the spring and have been circulating through the trade press since.

sections.h: Priced like commissions, not SKUs

p.text: "Jewelry has always been a form of cultural exploration," Furmanovich has said, and the collection wears that thesis openly, treating a brooch as a small piece of cabinetry and a cuff as a field for inlay.
The approach does not scale the way a diamond line does, which is precisely the point; each piece is closer to a commissioned object than a stocked SKU, and priced accordingly.

hero.bars_cap: Q2 output by mine · million carats

changed.text: The headline number from De Beers' second-quarter production report, published July 23, looks like a recovery: 7.8 million carats out of the ground, up 88% on the same quarter a year ago, when the miner had throttled output to defend prices. First-half production reached 14.91 million carats, up 46%.

means.text: A miner that digs 88% more and earns 44% less is not recovering; it is clearing its throat before a sale. The production rebound flatters a comparison against a year De Beers spent holding stones back, and the Venetia pause tells you management still does not trust the market to absorb the goods.

For a buyer, the appeal is the brand and the reserves, not this quarter's tape. For the trade, the signal is simpler: rough is cheap and getting cheaper, and the company that sets the price has stopped pretending otherwise.

visual.cap: Table I · Q2 output by mine · million carats
visual.note: Q2 2026 rough output by source · total 7.8M ct Where the carats came from: De Beers Q2 output by mine. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/103

sections.h: Eighty-eight percent more carats is the flattering number

p.text: Botswana did the heavy lifting, raising output 107% to 5.5 million carats; Venetia in South Africa added 700,000 carats, up 24%; Gahcho Kué in Canada contributed a million; only Namibia, at half a million carats, held flat. On the mine plan, this is a business running closer to capacity again.

p.lead: The price line tells the opposite story.
p.text: The average realised price fell 32% year on year to $105 a carat, and De Beers' rough price index, its measure of like-for-like pricing, was down 16%.

Second-quarter sales reached 7.1 million carats, but revenue from them fell 44% to $665 million; first-half rough revenue was $1.31 billion, down 23%. Producing more into a market that pays less is the arithmetic of a company that has decided inventory on the balance sheet is worse than stones sold cheaply.

sections.h: The price line is the honest one

p.lead: The guidance carries its own warning.
p.text: De Beers held full-year production guidance at 21 to 26 million carats, a wide band that already builds in planned maintenance and, more tellingly, an expected pause at Venetia in the second half.

The mine that just posted a 24% output gain is scheduled to go quiet, a reminder that the 88% rebound is measured against a deliberately starved 2025 rather than against health. Lab-grown competition, the company noted, continues to press the lower-value end of the book while premium goods hold firmer.

sections.h: The real story is a business dressed for sale

p.lead: Around the production report sits the larger question of ownership.
p.text: Anglo American, De Beers' parent, has flagged that underlying earnings at the diamond unit will be negative for the first half and has repeated that it is progressing the sale of the business while cutting costs.

Reports last week named a consortium led by former De Beers chief executive Gareth Penny as the front-runner to buy the 85% stake, though Anglo has declined to confirm. A full-year 2025 earnings loss of $511 million is the backdrop against which any buyer is doing its sums.

hero.bars_cap: September hike odds · market-implied

changed.text: Gold spent Friday doing what it has done for most of July: defending a line. Spot bullion changed hands near $4,028 an ounce, a slender margin above the $4,000 level that has become the market's psychological floor, after sliding through the back half of the week from a two-week peak above $4,160.

means.text: A metal that will not fall on higher rates and will not rally on a war premium is a metal in equilibrium, and equilibrium at $4,000 is its own kind of statement. The September meeting is now the hinge; an 80% hike bet is close enough to consensus that a hold would jolt gold up and a hike is largely in the price.
For the bench, plan around $4,000 as the floor it has earned, not the ceiling it once was.

visual.note: Fed-funds futures probability of a September rate rise The repricing that pins gold: September hike odds. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/104

sections.h: Gold is not falling, and it is not running

p.text: The metal is caught between two forces that rarely pull the same way, and this week they are pulling hard in opposite directions.

p.lead: On one side is the safe-haven bid.
p.text: Brent crude pushed above $100 a barrel as geopolitical risk, a widening conflict around Iran and strikes on shipping in the Gulf, fed straight into energy prices. Oil at three figures is an inflation input, and inflation is, in the long run, gold's friend.
Central banks agree with the thesis: roughly 45% of those surveyed say they intend to add gold over the coming year, a structural bid that does not blink at a single week's tape.

sections.h: Two forces, pulling in opposite directions

p.text: On the other side is the cost of holding a metal that pays no coupon. The same oil-driven inflation scare has pushed the two-year Treasury toward a seventeen-month high and the ten-year to 4.70%, and it has moved the market's read on the Federal Reserve.

Fed-funds futures now imply an 80% probability of a rate increase in September, up from 68% a week ago. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of gold, and that is the weight currently pinning it just above $4,000 rather than letting it run.

sections.h: September is the hinge

p.text: The white metals, quieter, carried the week's marks into Friday with little conviction: silver near $58.90 an ounce, platinum around $1,629 and palladium near $1,275, none of them moving enough to verify a fresh print.

For a jeweller costing a collection, the number that matters is not the daily wiggle but the shape: gold has spent a month refusing to break either way, and a $4,000 handle has held through a war premium, a hot inflation scare and a hawkish Fed repricing.

hero.bars_cap: Nine months on · US$ millions
hero.n: Apollo Gallery, Musée du Louvre, Paris

changed.text: The Louvre reopened its Apollo Gallery to the public on July 22, nine months after the October 2025 heist that turned the most famous jewel room in the world into a crime scene. Visitors filed back beneath the gilded ceiling to find the cases that once held the French crown jewels empty.

means.text: The Louvre's real decision this week was not to reopen the room but to empty it, and that is the more honest response. A gallery that cannot protect the crown jewels should not hold them, and moving them to a vault concedes what nine months of investigation confirmed, that display and security had drifted too far apart.

The wider bill lands on every institution that borrows historic jewels to draw a crowd; insurers and lenders will now price the Apollo raid into every loan agreement. Prestige, it turns out, has a security deposit.

visual.cap: Table I · Nine months on · US$ millions
visual.note: French royal jewels, October 2025 heist The ledger of a heist: taken against recovered. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/105

sections.h: The room reopened; the jewels did not

p.text: The museum has decided the gallery will no longer display royal jewellery at all; the surviving pieces are being moved to a more secure location, and the Apollo reverts to its older function as a state gallery.
The raid it is recovering from was a study in speed.

A crew disguised as construction workers parked a truck-mounted basket lift against the building's river façade, rode it to a first-floor window, cut through with an angle grinder and a disc cutter, lifted jewelled pieces valued at more than $100 million from their cases, and were back on motorcycles in roughly seven minutes.
It was less a burglary than a logistics exercise, executed against a national museum in daylight.

sections.h: Seven minutes against a national museum

p.lead: The investigation has produced arrests but no jewels.
p.text: Four suspects are in custody; by the account reported this week, they say they were hired hands and have declined to name whoever commissioned the theft.

No stones have been recovered, and the working assumption across the trade is grim: pieces this recognisable are worth far more broken and recut than intact, which means the French crown jewels may already have ceased to exist as the objects the catalogue describes.

sections.h: The bill lands on everyone who lends a stone

p.lead: The reopening doubles as a policy moment.
p.text: France's culture ministry has announced a national plan to harden security at museums and national collections, an admission that the vulnerability was systemic rather than local. The art-recovery specialist Christopher Marinello put the lesson bluntly: if thieves can get into the Louvre, they can get in anywhere.
For a jewellery trade that leans on museums to display, authenticate and lend prestige to historic stones, that is an uncomfortable sentence to sit under.

hero.bars_cap: Clearance · percent of book sold

changed.text: Gemfields' latest auction of higher-quality rough emeralds closed at $26.8 million, a result the miner will take as a steadying hand under a jittery colour market.

means.text: $146 a carat with a 99%-by-weight clearance is a genuinely good number, and it says the ceiling of the colour market is intact even as the middle sags. But read the ruby decision and the rupee line together and the picture sharpens: this is a producer rationing supply to protect price because it cannot afford a weak print.
Emeralds held the line this week. Whether rubies get the same disciplined treatment, or get pushed to market to plug a hole, is the number the desk will be watching next.

visual.cap: Table I · Clearance · percent of book sold
visual.note: Kagem higher-quality emerald auction, London A near-total clearance: the emerald book sold through. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/106

sections.h: The ceiling of the colour market is holding

p.text: Held in London over 4 to 21 May and reported in recent days, the sale cleared 36 of its 37 lots, 97% by number and 99% by weight, at an average of $146.08 a carat.
In a year when almost every hard-luxury category has been marked down, an emerald book that sells through at those prices reads as quiet strength.
The stones come from Kagem, the Zambian mine Gemfields owns 75%, with the Industrial Development Corporation of Zambia holding the rest.

Adrian Banks, the company's managing director of product and sales, framed the demand as real but cautious: appetite for higher-quality emeralds remains stable, he said, while the market exercises a degree of caution against a backdrop of geopolitical tension and macro uncertainty. The caveat had a currency attached.

The Indian rupee has lost roughly 10% against the dollar since September 2025, and India is where much of the world's rough colour is cut; a weaker rupee makes every dollar-priced lot dearer at the bench.

sections.h: What Gemfields is not selling matters too

p.text: What Gemfields did not do this cycle is as telling as what it did. The company has been holding back on rubies, pacing its higher-value ruby offering rather than forcing goods into an uncertain room.

That is a producer managing scarcity deliberately, the colour-market equivalent of De Beers keeping rough in the vault, except that Gemfields is doing it from a position of financial strain rather than strength.

sections.h: A good auction does not erase a bad year

p.lead: The strain is real.
p.text: Gemfields posted a $51 million loss for 2025, and it has spent this year raising capital and trimming to steady the balance sheet. An emerald sale that performs is oxygen, but a single strong auction does not reverse a loss of that size.

The read across the colour trade is that the top of the market, signed, high-clarity, provenance-backed stones, is holding, while the broader book waits on the same macro clouds hanging over diamonds and watches.

hero.bars_cap: RapNet June move by size · percent

changed.text: The recovery in polished diamonds, such as it is, keeps arriving from the bottom of the size chart. The RapNet Diamond Index for June, published mid-July, rose 4.2% for 0.30-carat stones and 1.3% for half-carats, each an acceleration on May's gains. The three-carat category edged up 0.4%, turning positive after a soft spring.

means.text: A 4.2% monthly gain in half-point goods sounds like spring, but a recovery built on empty shelves is a fragile thing, and the 0.7% dip in one-carat stones is the tell. The size that anchors the bridal counter is still drifting, and that is the number that pays the trade's rent.

Until the one-carat line turns on real demand rather than the small end turning on thin inventory, the desk reads this as stabilisation, not recovery, the diamond market holding its breath, not catching it.

visual.cap: Table I · RapNet June move by size · percent
visual.note: June RapNet move by size · 1.00-ct fell 0.7% The recovery arrives from the small end: RapNet, June. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/107

sections.h: The gains keep coming from the smallest goods

p.text: The exception sat in the middle of the counter: the one-carat benchmark, the size most shoppers picture when they picture a diamond, slipped 0.7%.

p.lead: The mechanism matters more than the percentages.
p.text: Rapaport attributes the firmness in smalls to inventory reductions rather than a wave of new buying; dealers have stopped restocking melee and small goods, and the thinner shelves are letting prices correct upward.
It is a supply story dressed as a demand story, the market clearing an overhang rather than discovering fresh appetite. Prices rise because there is less to sell, not because more people are buying.

sections.h: Thin shelves, not fresh demand

p.lead: The size split is its own signal about who is spending.
p.text: Larger goods, two carats and up in the G-to-I colour, VS-to-SI clarity band, remained the strongest sellers in the United States, the province of buyers less troubled by the macro clouds. Rounds in the one-to-two-carat range showed what Rapaport called only mild improvement.
The barbell that has defined the polished market all year is still there: the top holds, the entry firms on scarcity, and the mass-market middle where most engagement rings live stays soft.

sections.h: The one-carat line is the one that pays the rent

p.text: Set against De Beers' rough report the same week, the polished tape completes a coherent picture. Rough is being produced in volume and sold cheap; polished is recovering only where supply has been deliberately choked. Neither half of the pipeline is being pulled higher by consumers reaching for diamonds.
Both are being managed, by miners holding grades back and by dealers refusing to restock, into the appearance of stability.
