hero.bars_cap: Lab-grown discount to natural · percent

changed.text: The gap between a natural diamond and its laboratory twin has become a canyon. Analysing appraisal and insurance records from March 2019 through May 2025, the insurance-technology firm BriteCo found lab-grown diamonds now priced roughly 73% below comparable naturals. In 2019 the discount was 26.6%.

means.text: The lab-grown industry made a bet that price was the whole game, and winning on price turns out to have been the losing move. At a 73% discount the grown stone has priced itself into a different product category, beautiful, honest, and no longer competing for the meaning a buyer wants an engagement ring to carry.
Naturals reclaiming the ring is not nostalgia; it is what happens when one side of a market keeps cutting price until the cut becomes the message. The number to watch is not the discount.
It is the share.

visual.cap: Table I · Lab-grown discount to natural · percent
visual.note: Lab-grown price discount to natural · BriteCo appraisal data Six years, a canyon: the lab-grown discount. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/108

sections.h: The discount is now a canyon

p.lead: By 2025 it had widened to 72.8%.
p.text: A one-carat natural averages around $4,200 in the data; its grown equivalent sells for about $1,000 or less.

p.lead: The widening is a supply story with a demand twist.
p.text: Grown-diamond output from Chinese and Indian producers has climbed relentlessly, and a manufactured good made in ever-greater volume behaves the way manufactured goods do: the price falls toward the cost of making it.

Natural prices, having spiked through the pandemic years, have drifted back down but nothing like as far. The two lines have been diverging for six years, and the distance between them is now the widest it has ever been.

sections.h: Cheaper did not mean winning

p.lead: Here is the twist the grown-diamond industry did not script.
p.text: As lab-grown got cheaper, it did not consolidate its grip on the bridal market; it started to lose it.
BriteCo's data has natural stones back to 57.3% of engagement rings sold in late 2024 and early 2025, a reversal from a lab-grown peak of 47.7% share.
The cheaper the grown stone became, the more it read to some shoppers as a fashion purchase rather than an heirloom, and an engagement ring is the last place many buyers want to feel they economised.

sections.h: Price was never the whole game

p.lead: For retailers the divergence is a margin puzzle with no clean answer.
p.text: A grown-diamond sale is a smaller ticket that keeps shrinking as wholesale prices fall, which is why several chains have hedged by selling both and steering the emotional pitch toward natural.

The risk is a two-tier counter that trains the customer to see the grown stone as the discount option and the natural as the real one, useful for natural margins, corrosive for the grown-diamond brand the same store spent five years building.

hero.bars_cap: The night's top lots · US$ millions · 13 June 2025

changed.lead: The trophy end of the jewellery market is still doing the work.
changed.text: Sotheby's High Jewelry sale in New York on 13 June 2025 made $31.4 million with 95% of lots finding buyers, a result led, as these sales almost always are, by a handful of exceptional single stones rather than broad depth.

means.text: $31.4 million at 95% sold is a strong night, but read it with the withdrawn pink and the lesson is precision, not exuberance. The market for singular, provenance-backed stones is genuinely intact; the market for aggressively estimated ones is not.

Collectors are still paying for rarity they can name, a Kashmir sapphire, a Burmese ruby, a signed JAR, and passing on anything that feels priced for a hotter year than this one. The trophies carry the room.
They no longer forgive a reserve set in the mood of the year before.

visual.cap: Table I · The night's top lots · US$ millions · 13 June 2025
visual.note: Sotheby's New York High Jewelry · 13 June 2025 What money still chases: the night's top five. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/109

sections.h: The very top is a different economy

p.text: That night is a marker rather than a bulletin, and it is read here as one: the sale it belongs to is more than a year behind the tape this paper prints each morning, and the room described below is the room of that June, not of this one.

p.lead: The board read like a tour of what money still chases.
p.text: A Graff ring set with a 35-carat D-colour diamond took $3.2 million. A Marcus & Co. sautoir centred on a 9.6-carat Burmese ruby and a 2.02-carat fancy vivid blue diamond tied at $1.8 million apiece.

A JAR ring holding an 8.62-carat Colombian emerald made $1.6 million, and a 1930s Kashmir sapphire ring of 7.5 carats reached $1.4 million. Colour, provenance and signature, the three things a factory cannot print, carried the night.

sections.h: Colour, provenance, signature

p.lead: Sotheby's framed it as continuity.
p.text: Quig Bruning, the house's head of jewellery in the Americas, said provenance, rarity and exceptional craftsmanship continue to ignite the passions of collectors, and called the sale a great continuation of what he described as a phenomenal year for jewellery.
The house has reason for the confidence: at the level where a single stone clears seven figures, the buyer pool has barely noticed the macro weather that has chilled the retail counter.

sections.h: But a too-high estimate still walks

p.lead: The counter-example was a short walk away, on the same week's calendar.
p.text: Phillips withdrew the top lot of its own New York jewels sale, a 3.03-carat fancy intense pink diamond estimated at $1.2 million to $1.6 million, after bids failed to meet the reserve.

A withdrawn headline lot is the auction world's quiet way of saying the estimate and the room disagreed, and it is a useful corrective to any story that the top is invincible. Even at the summit, price discovery still bites when a house aims too high.

hero.bars_cap: Growth is back · percent

changed.text: The Swiss watch industry got its best headline in a year last week: exports rose 11.2% in June, according to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, an unexpected rebound after months of soft numbers, and Swatch Group shares jumped on the read-through.

means.text: An 11.2% export rebound is worth having, but a half-percent net margin is the number that tells you what kind of rebound it is. Volume returning to the wholesale pipe is not the same as customers returning to the counter, and until the pre-owned market turns and the profit line thickens, the desk treats June as a base effect flattered by restocking rather than proof the storm has passed.
The exports came back first. The margin, and the resale tape, will say whether they meant it.

visual.cap: Table I · Growth is back · percent
visual.note: Top line up, profit flat — Swatch H1, FHS June The rebound that skips the bottom line. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/110

sections.h: The best watch headline in a year

p.text: After a year in which the standard question was how much worse it could get, a double-digit export gain landed like a change of season.

Look past the shipment figure, though, and the profit line refuses to celebrate. Swatch Group's first-half revenue was CHF 3.12 billion, up about 9% at constant currency, with the United States up 27% and China including Hong Kong and Macau up 9%.
Net profit for the same six months was CHF 16 million, roughly half a percent of sales.

A company can grow its top line smartly and still hand almost none of it to the bottom, and that is precisely what a mass-and-mid-market watchmaker does when it is discounting to move stock and carrying the cost of a bloated inventory.

sections.h: The profit line refuses to celebrate

p.text: The divergence maps onto a split that has defined the whole watch year: shipments and sell-through are not the same thing. Exports measure what leaves Switzerland for the wholesale channel; they can rise on restocking and a soft base without a single extra watch reaching a wrist.

The pre-owned market, the truest read on end demand, has yet to confirm the rebound; resale values for the most-traded references remain well below their 2022 peak, and a genuine recovery would show up there before it showed up in a profit statement.

sections.h: Shipments are not sell-through

p.lead: Underneath the group averages, the money is moving to the edges.
p.text: Independent makers with waiting lists keep their pricing power while several group-owned brands fight discounting; the strongest markets are the ones, like the United States, where wealthy buyers are insulated from the macro weather.
The June export jump is real and welcome, but it is a wholesale-channel event, and the channel has been wrong-footed before by reading its own restocking as demand.

bars.l: Brazil — Loose Polished Color, In Force

hero.bars_cap: The jewelry tariff wall, points of duty

changed.text: The tariff wall that has been rising around American jewelry counters all summer just gained its most surprising section: the northern one. A 50% tariff on Canadian imports, enacted under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, takes effect August 19, thirty days after signing.

means.who: The maple-leaf premium just became a maple-leaf surcharge.
means.text: Canadian-cut stones were the ethical-sourcing story American retail told its most careful customers, and at plus-fifty they will be nearly unsellable against identical goods cut in Surat from the same Canadian rough.

A tariff that exempts the ore and taxes the craftsmanship does not protect anyone; it simply moves the cutting wheel offshore. The counters have four weeks to land goods, and the desk expects August's import data to show one of the strangest pull-forwards on record.

visual.cap: Table I · The jewelry tariff wall, points of duty
rows: Brazil — Loose Polished Color, In Force
visual.note: Rough rides free; the cutting wheel pays The wall, section by section. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/096

sections.h: Six codes, thirty days

p.text: The order names six Harmonized Tariff Schedule codes that land squarely on the trade: loose polished diamonds (7102.39.00), semi-manufactured .995 silver including gold- and platinum-plated forms (7106.92.10), silver jewelry valued over $18 per dozen pieces (7113.11.50), gold necklaces and neck chains excluding rope and mixed-link (7113.19.29), precious-metal jewelry including plated goods (7113.19.50), and base-metal jewelry (7117.19.90).

sections.h: No shelter in the USMCA

p.lead: Two details make the order harsher than its headline.
p.text: First, the Jewelers Vigilance Committee notes the tariffs apply to the listed products even where they would qualify for duty-free treatment under the USMCA, the free-trade agreement Washington itself negotiated with Ottawa in the first Trump term.
Second, the new duty applies on top of existing tariffs rather than replacing them. A category that already carried a rate now carries that rate plus fifty points.

p.lead: The exemption is as pointed as the inclusion.
p.text: Rough diamonds are excluded, which means Canadian rough that leaves the Northwest Territories for cutting elsewhere enters the United States under the cutting country's rate, not Canada's.

What pays the 50% is the small, premium trade in stones actually polished in Canada, the traceable, mine-to-market goods sold for two decades under a maple-leaf promise. The order effectively taxes the value Canada adds and waves through the value it exports raw.

sections.h: From repeal to carve-outs

p.lead: The industry's response has settled into weary procedure.
p.text: Jewelers of America president David Bonaparte, who has spent the season filing exemption requests for diamond, gemstone and pearl codes, framed the situation plainly: "President Trump has stated that tariffs are here to stay". The lobbying goal has shrunk accordingly, from repeal to carve-outs, code by code.
Canada joins Brazil, whose 25% duty on loose polished colored stones is now in force, and the roughly 46 countries facing a proposed 12.5% rate on colored gemstones and pearls by month-end.

hero.bars_cap: Three tracks, one month · the 301 docket

changed.text: The colored-stone trade now has a number to dread and a date to watch.

means.text: Color spent two decades as the affordable, story-rich alternative to the diamond counter, and its supply chain, artisanal, multi-country, thinly capitalized, is the least equipped in the industry to absorb a demand shock at the border. Twelve and a half points will not close Thailand's cutting houses, but it will quietly reprice every American jeweler's fall reorder.
Watch July 24: if the 10% surcharge dies quietly and 12.5% arrives loudly, the net change is small and the headlines will be wrong in both directions.

visual.cap: Table I · Three tracks, one month · the 301 docket
visual.note: Bar for the subsidies review indicates an open question, not a rate The color trade's month of rulings. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/097

sections.h: A number and a date

p.text: The US Trade Representative's expedited Section 301 investigation into colored gemstones and cultured pearls has produced preliminary findings proposing a 12.5% tariff on imports from roughly 46 countries, a list that includes every sourcing capital that matters: India, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Australia among them.
Final resolution is expected by the end of July, which gives the trade roughly a week of certainty about its uncertainty.

p.lead: It is one of three tracks running at once.
p.text: A second review covering subsidies and industrial policies spans 16 trading partners, including Thailand, Cambodia, India, Japan and the European Union, and is due to resolve later in July.

The third, aimed at Brazil, has already concluded: a definitive 25% tariff on loose polished colored gemstones from the country that supplies much of the world's tourmaline, aquamarine and emerald, which this page covered as it took effect this week.
Rough Brazilian stones stay exempt, in the same rough-in, polished-pays logic that now governs the Canadian diamond order.

sections.h: One deadline runs the other way

p.lead: One deadline cuts the other way.
p.text: The temporary 10% global import surcharge, the blanket duty that has sat over nearly everything since spring, expires July 24.

If it lapses as scheduled while the 12.5% proposal is still pending, the color trade will briefly enjoy something close to its historic footing, a window importers with goods in transit will not need to be told twice about.

sections.h: Nothing domestic to protect

p.text: The American Gem Trade Association's argument against the whole exercise is that a protective tariff needs something to protect. The United States has effectively no commercial colored-stone mining or cutting industry; AGTA argues loose colored gemstones should keep their historic duty-free status because there is "no meaningful domestic production".
A Section 301 remedy with no domestic industry behind it functions as a straightforward consumption tax on sapphire engagement rings and pearl strands, paid at American counters.

hero.bars_cap: The week's gold prints, dollars an ounce

changed.text: The rally that started with Tuesday's $144 run met its counterparty on Thursday, and the counterparty was a barrel of crude. Spot gold traded at $4,103.39 an ounce by 0713 GMT, down 0.6% on the session and roughly $60 below Wednesday's two-week peak of $4,165.87.

means.who: A 0.6% pullback after a $144 two-day run is consolidation, not verdict.
means.text: The number that matters is 77, the September hike probability, because gold at $4,100 has never coexisted with a genuine tightening cycle and one of them eventually has to give.
The desk notes that 'at least one hike by year-end' was also the consensus in three previous episodes this cycle, and the hikes never came. Respect the odds; remember their record.

sections.h: The counterparty is crude

p.lead: August futures sat at $4,106.40, off 1.1%.
p.text: The proximate cause was not the dollar, which actually eased 0.1%, but oil, which climbed to its highest level in more than six weeks and dragged inflation expectations up with it.

p.lead: The transmission mechanism ran through the rates market.
p.text: Two-year Treasury yields climbed to a 17-month high, and the CME FedWatch tool now assigns a 77% probability to a rate hike in September, with futures broadly positioned for at least one increase by year-end.

Next week's meeting, July 28 and 29, is expected to produce no change; it is the meetings after that the tape is repricing. Jigar Trivedi of IndusInd Securities captured the bind: "Oil continues to be up, adding to pressures of inflation".

sections.h: The complex steps down together

p.lead: The white metals followed gold down the stairs.
p.text: Silver traded $58.90, off 1.3% from a week that had touched $60.11; platinum eased 1.0% to $1,628.63 and palladium 1.2% to $1,274.96, both giving back a slice of Tuesday's outsized gains.
Nothing in the complex broke anything that matters: gold remains more than $100 above Monday's $4,000.30 close, and every metal on the board is still carrying most of the week's advance.

sections.h: The loop, named

p.lead: The strange loop in the setup deserves naming.
p.text: The same Middle East risk that buys gold its haven bid is now selling it back through the oil market: crude strength feeds inflation, inflation feeds hike odds, and hike odds raise the cost of holding an asset that pays nothing.
Tuesday's move was the war premium arriving; Thursday's is the second-order consequence of the same war, routed through the Fed. Until one of those channels dominates, the tape will keep doing this.

hero.bars_cap: Where the half grew · reported gains, percent

changed.lead: Swatch Group's half-year report reads like two different companies stapled together.
changed.text: The top line belongs to a business in recovery: revenue of CHF 3.12 billion ($3.84 billion), up 2% as reported and 9% at constant exchange rates, with watches and jewelry contributing CHF 2.95 billion.

means.text: Nine percent constant-currency growth is a genuine recovery; sixteen million francs of profit is a rounding error wearing a suit. The group is effectively running the world's most prestigious watch factories at break-even and calling it a turnaround, which it is, but only in the way that a patient sitting up in bed is a recovery.
The China number is the one to keep: if 9% growth there holds through the second half, the margin will follow. If it doesn't, the franc will still be Swiss.

visual.cap: Table I · Where the half grew · reported gains, percent
visual.note: South Korea +12, Australia +5; India, Mexico and Saudi Arabia cited for strong gains The recovery map. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/099

sections.h: The top line recovers

p.lead: The regional detail is better still.
p.text: The United States gained 27%, Japan 20%, Spain 28%, Italy 12%, South Korea 12%, and China including Hong Kong and Macau, the market whose collapse has defined the group's last three years, turned in growth of 9%.

sections.h: The bottom line hasn't

p.lead: The bottom line belongs to a company still on the operating table.
p.text: Net profit fell 6% to CHF 16 million ($19.7 million), which against CHF 3.12 billion of sales works out to a net margin of roughly half a percent.

The seven-point gap between reported and constant-currency growth names the culprit: the Swiss franc, which converts foreign revenue into fewer francs while the group's cost base, factories, watchmakers, headquarters, stays resolutely Swiss and resolutely franc-denominated.

The group, which owns Omega, Tissot, Longines and Harry Winston among seventeen brands, chose to lead its outlook with momentum rather than margin. It anticipates stronger growth in the second half, citing "stronger sales in May and June, which continued into the first weeks of July".
New product launches and improved retail efficiency get credit for the positive results; high-potential markets, India, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, are singled out for particularly strong gains.

sections.h: The export tape agrees

p.text: The report lands three days after the federation's June export data showed Swiss shipments up 11.2%, with the US and UK both up double digits, and confirms what that tape implied: the demand turn is real, broad and accelerating into July.
What the export numbers could not show, and Swatch's accounts do, is how little of that demand survives the journey from Geneva showroom to Biel income statement when the franc is this strong.

hero.bars_cap: The deficit, shrinking · CAD millions

changed.text: Birks Group's fiscal 2026 is what a repair year looks like when it works: still red, but three-quarters less of it. The Montreal jeweler posted a net loss of CAD 3.4 million ($2.4 million) for the year ended March 28, against CAD 12.8 million ($9.1 million) a year earlier, a 73% reduction.

means.text: A 73% smaller loss is direction, not destination; CAD 3.4 million of red ink on CAD 205 million of sales means the model is one strong quarter from working and one weak one from doubling the deficit again. The comp number is the honest one, and 2.6% in this gold market is modest.
The Oakridge store is the bet to watch: house-brand mono-retail is where the margin is, and Birks has the name to try it.

visual.cap: Table I · The deficit, shrinking · CAD millions
visual.note: A 73% reduction in the annual deficit, on sales up 15.5% The repair year, charted. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/100

sections.h: Red, but three-quarters less

p.text: Sales rose 15.5% to CAD 205.4 million ($145.7 million), and comparable-store sales, the number that strips out acquisitions and flatters no one, gained 2.6%.

sections.h: One engine bought, one built

p.lead: The growth has two engines, one bought and one built.
p.text: The acquisition of European Boutique added scale, while Birks-branded jewelry, the house's own gold-and-diamond lines, grew organically alongside third-party jewelry sales.

Interim CEO Niccolò Rossi di Montelera said retail performance "outperformed over the prior year due to the strategic acquisition of European Boutique", crediting organic growth in the house brand alongside it.

The offset was third-party watches, which declined after a brand exited one of the company's stores, a reminder of how much Canadian luxury retail rides on distribution agreements it does not control.

The next move is expansion of the house's own name: a Birks mono-brand store opens this fall in Vancouver's Oakridge mall. For a 147-year-old company that has spent recent years as a multi-brand showcase, putting fresh capital into a store that sells only Birks is a quiet statement about where management believes the margin lives.

sections.h: The backdrop cuts both ways

p.lead: The macro backdrop cuts both ways.
p.text: Gold jewelry, a growing share of what Birks sells under its own name, has been the category of the year everywhere bullion has run.

But the company reports in a country that just became the target of a 50% American tariff on jewelry and polished diamonds; Birks' retail is domestic, so the direct exposure is limited, yet the trade war now reshaping its home market's currency and cross-border shopping patterns is nobody's friend.

sections.h: A lemon, by special order

p.text: The lemon wears 0.46 carats of yellow diamonds and 0.48 carats of yellow sapphires over 18-karat yellow gold, with tsavorite leaves and a white-diamond stem, and splits on its hinge to reveal white-diamond seeds.

sections.h: The cheaper branches

p.text: The cherry, at $10,985, is the entry point: 2.65 carats of ruby pavé with diamond accents, opening to a 0.75-carat cabochon garnet, a stone-in-fruit conceit executed with a straight face.

The pear, at $14,500, is the colorist's piece, layering a 3.50-carat yellow sapphire with orange sapphire, peridot and 1.36 carats of tsavorite, and concealing five pear-shaped garnets totaling 1.72 carats.

p.text: The fruits arrive into a market that has been rewarding exactly this kind of object.

Graff's twelve butterfly jabot pins, Pomellato's mandala capsule and the general brooch-and-objet revival this page has tracked all season point the same direction: at the top of the market, jewelry is drifting from adornment toward miniature sculpture, and houses are competing on mechanics, hinges, tremblant wings, hidden compartments, as much as on carats.

hero.bars_cap: The crown's partner doors · counts

changed.text: The Washington suburbs now have a Rolex address to match their tax bracket. Liljenquist & Beckstead opened a 2,800-square-foot Rolex boutique on July 22 along the main corridor of the recently renovated Tysons Galleria in McLean, Virginia, the fourth location for a family firm that has sold jewelry in the capital's orbit since 1978.

means.text: A visible workshop is the smartest square footage in watch retail; it converts a waiting-room chore into proof of competence, and proof of competence into the thing Rolex actually rations, trust. The dependency question is real but academic: no family jeweler has ever gotten smaller by building the crown a nicer room.

The desk notes the address, a renovated luxury mall rather than a Manhattan avenue, and reads it as the American watch market's actual center of gravity: the affluent suburb, not the flagship district.

sections.h: An address to match the bracket

p.text: Lisa Colen, the company's director of operations, called it "a distinguished home for Rolex in the Mid-Atlantic".

sections.h: The build is the point

p.lead: The build is the point.
p.text: A sawtooth storefront in bronze and brass gives way to American walnut ceilings and walls, travertine-framed display windows and a lounge with private and semi-private consultation rooms.

The theatrical centerpiece is a Rolex-trained watchmaking workshop set behind glass, with a dry bar positioned so customers can watch a movement being serviced while they wait. Service, the least glamorous half of the watch business, has been promoted to the shop window.

sections.h: Fewer doors, grander ones

p.text: The opening extends a pattern this page has been logging all year: the crown's retail footprint is consolidating into fewer, grander doors operated by its most trusted partners. Beaverbrooks just converted a 165-year-old Sheffield showroom into its fourth Rolex-anchored boutique; the brand's certified pre-owned program keeps pulling secondary-market demand into the same authorized rooms.
For independent jewelers, a dedicated Rolex boutique is simultaneously the best franchise in retail and a deepening dependency on a single Geneva landlord.

hero.bars_cap: One Tuesday, dollars an ounce · gold
hero.src: Tuesday's board, Kitco, late New York

changed.lead: The quiet week lasted one session.
changed.text: On Monday gold closed at $4,000.30 and this desk wrote that the tape had nothing to do but wait for the July 28-29 Fed meeting. On Tuesday the market disagreed.

means.text: A $144 range in one day is not a trend, and Tuesday's short-covering can unwind as fast as it arrived. But the floor at $3,964 has now been tested three times and bought three times, and the first big move off it went up, not down.
The waiting room emptied early. The meeting will tell us whether it refills.

visual.cap: Table I · One Tuesday, dollars an ounce · gold
visual.note: Nearly $144 between the session's low and high prints The quiet week, cancelled. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/087

sections.h: One session of quiet

p.text: By late evening in New York, Kitco's board showed spot gold at $4,131.00, up $54.30 on the session, or 1.33%, after a run that touched $3,998.80 at the low and $4,142.70 at the high. Between those two prints, gold traveled nearly $144 inside a day, and finished roughly $130 above Monday's close.

p.lead: The push came from the usual two hands working together.
p.text: Kitco's Tuesday market report credited "short covering and renewed haven demand" for the move, with the US-Iran conflict lifting crude oil for another session and money returning to metal even as Treasury yields rose and the dollar firmed.
That last part is the notable piece of the arithmetic: gold rallying through a firmer dollar is a sign of demand that is not waiting for the currency math to cooperate.

sections.h: The white metals run harder

p.lead: The white metals ran harder than the yellow one.
p.text: Silver settled at $59.64, up 1.67%, after touching $60.11 at the high, a level it last saw before the June selloff carved the price back to the mid-fifties. Platinum added 2.28% to $1,660 and traded as high as $1,676.
Palladium rose 2.85% to $1,297, with a $1,347 print at the top of its range. Whatever the complex was waiting for last week, all four metals decided on Tuesday that it had arrived early.

sections.h: A hot tape into a hold

p.text: For the jewelry trade, the move re-prices the counter again, and it does so a week before the Fed provides any cover for it. A bench buying gold at $4,131 on Wednesday is working $130 above Monday's cost, and the retailers who report next week will be asked, again, whether the customer keeps absorbing it.

The early evidence from Asia, in Luk Fook's quarter published this week, is that she does. The July 28-29 meeting now arrives with the tape hot rather than flat, which changes the stakes of a hold: a Fed that does nothing into a rising gold market is, for this trade, a Fed that did something.

changed.text: The most striking number in the World Gold Council's July update on India is not a price. It is a proportion: at some retailers, old-gold exchanges now make up as much as 70% of jewelry sales.

means.who: India is often described as the world's price-taker in gold.
means.text: This summer it looks more like a closed loop, selling itself its own metal at a narrowing discount.

For the global market the message is subtle but real: when the world's second-largest consumer meets a rally with recycled supply rather than fresh imports, the marginal ounce has to find its buyer somewhere else.

sections.h: The cupboard is the mine

p.text: The customer walks in with her grandmother's bangles and walks out with a new set, and the till records a sale that required almost no new metal at all.
Kavita Chacko's market report, published July 17, describes a market that has responded to four-thousand-dollar gold not by leaving the counter but by feeding it from the household vault.

sections.h: A correction that felt like a rally

p.lead: The price backdrop explains the behavior.
p.text: International gold fell more than 11% in June to around $4,000 an ounce before stabilizing in July, and domestic prices declined roughly 10% to near 141,000 rupees per ten grams.
The year-to-date split is stranger: international prices are down 7% in 2026, but Indian domestic prices have gained 6%, propped up by a May import-duty increase and a softer rupee.
Indian households, in other words, have watched local gold get more expensive even through a global correction, and the rational response has been to monetize the metal already in the cupboard.

p.lead: Demand did not disappear; it changed shape.
p.text: Retailers reported April-June revenue growth of 30-60% year over year as the June price dip pulled buyers in. Gold ETFs took in 34.4 billion rupees in June, the strongest month since February, and digital gold purchases reached a three-month high of 25.5 billion rupees in transaction value.
Bars and coins, the classic price-chasing trade, cooled as softer prices made the momentum case harder to tell.

sections.h: The loop closes

p.lead: The recycling wave shows up in the trade accounts.
p.text: Gold imports fell 42% month over month to $1.97 billion in June, the lowest reading since June 2025, with estimated volumes of just 16-22 tonnes.

With scrap supplying the counters, the domestic discount to international prices narrowed from a peak of $150 an ounce in May to about $40 by mid-July. A market that once imported its demand is, for now, circulating it.

hero.src: Luk Fook, three months to June 30

changed.lead: Luk Fook's first fiscal quarter reads like two companies filing one report.
changed.text: For the three months to June 30, the Hong Kong jeweler's retail sales rose 32% year over year and group same-store sales gained 39%, with Hong Kong and Macau up 41% and the mainland up 22%.

means.text: Yesterday this desk wrote that Hong Kong's gold counters were running hot; today the ledgers confirm it, and put a number on the cost. A 50% gold quarter and a minus-58% mainland diamond quarter are the same fact seen from two sides.

The wedding stone has lost the argument for the mainland customer's wallet, and the bullion counter has won it. Retailers everywhere should read those two numbers together before planning next year's showcase.

visual.cap: Table I · Same-store sales, April–June · percent change, year on year
visual.note: Bars show magnitude; diamonds moved down, gold moved up One report, two businesses. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/089

sections.h: Two companies, one filing

p.text: Strip out the shine, though, and the quarter splits cleanly along product lines: gold same-store sales surged 50%, while diamond same-store sales fell 17%. On the mainland, the diamond number was a startling minus 58%.

sections.h: The customer stopped waiting

p.lead: The gold side of the ledger no longer even blames the price.
p.text: Same-store gold sales rose 55% in Hong Kong and Macau and 21% on the mainland, and the company observed that "consumers have gradually adapted to the high gold price environment".

That is the quiet capitulation the trade has been waiting three years to hear: the customer has stopped treating four-thousand-dollar gold as a reason to wait, and started treating it as the reason to buy.

Across town, Chow Sang Sang told the same story at a lower amplitude. Retail sales value rose 16% for the June quarter, with same-store sales up 17% in China and 30% in Hong Kong and Macau, driven by steady local demand and returning tourist traffic.
Gold jewelry held its bid throughout; the company credited its signature collections for keeping customers at the counter through the price swings.

sections.h: Fewer, better doors

p.lead: What neither company is doing is opening stores.
p.text: Luk Fook closed a net 148 locations in the quarter, taking its global count to 2,857, even as it opened a self-operated store in Singapore, launched a licensed shop in Vietnam, and penciled in 30 net new overseas stores across two more countries for the fiscal year.
Chow Sang Sang closed a net 49 shops in the first half, ending June at 776. The playbook on both sides is identical: fewer, better doors, and a counter that sells metal first.

hero.src: The consultation · who and what is on the table

changed.text: The response to Venetia arrived within days, and it was not conciliatory.

means.text: Every diamond-market downturn eventually stops being a price chart and becomes a payroll. The union's argument that the company saw this coming is hard to dismiss: this page has been charting the rough market's slide for months, and De Beers' own sight cuts told the same story.
The question for the new owners is whether Venetia's two years dark end in a restart or a eulogy. The workers have noticed that nobody will put the restart in writing.

visual.cap: Table I · The pause, in people · positions in Section 189A consultation
visual.note: Two years dark, with no restart in writing The payroll behind the price chart. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/090

sections.h: Not conciliatory

p.text: The National Union of Mineworkers, South Africa's largest mining union, has formally condemned De Beers' plan to halt production at the Venetia mine for two years, a move that places 1,214 workers into retrenchment consultation: 1,134 permanent mine employees and a further 80 at De Beers Sightholder Sales South Africa.
NUM's diamond-sector chief negotiator, Masibulele Naki, put the union's position in one line: "Workers cannot be treated as disposable tools".

sections.h: The charge is timing

p.lead: The union's sharpest charge is about timing, not economics.
p.text: De Beers, NUM argues, has known about the challenges confronting the diamond market for a long time, and yet presented the pause to the workforce as a sudden necessity, with dismissal notices issued before any meaningful engagement.
In the union's telling, the consultation now underway is theater around a decision already taken, and the company's communication before the announcement was close to nonexistent.

p.lead: NUM is not arguing that the diamond market's troubles are imaginary.
p.text: Its counterproposal accepts the pressure and redirects it: executive cost reviews before worker retrenchments, retraining programs for underground staff, and spending cuts that do not start at the bottom of the pay scale.

The union has pledged to use all available organizational, legal and collective bargaining channels to protect its members, which in South African labor practice can stretch a Section 189A process considerably.

sections.h: An awkward hour to be sold

p.lead: The fight lands at an awkward hour for the company.
p.text: De Beers is being sold; Anglo American has named Gareth Penny's consortium as preferred bidder, Botswana has negotiated its own stake upward, and the Venetia pause is part of the cost discipline that makes the asset presentable.

Venetia is South Africa's largest diamond mine and the country's principal remaining stake in an industry it once defined. A two-year pause with 1,214 jobs attached is, for the Limpopo towns around the pit, indistinguishable from a closure with a promise stapled to it.

hero.bars_cap: The one-carat question · indicative dollars per stone
hero.src: The Knot 2026 Real Weddings study and Q1 pricing

changed.text: The lab-grown debate has an official scoreboard now, and it is not close. According to The Knot's 2026 Real Weddings study, 61% of engagement rings bought by couples who married in 2025 carried lab-grown center stones.

means.text: The number that matters is not 61; it is whichever number comes next. If lab-grown's share plateaus here, the trade settles into Smith's bifurcation and both counters make money.

If it keeps climbing, the natural engagement stone becomes what the mechanical watch became: a luxury object justified by meaning rather than convention. The watch industry, it is worth noting, eventually found that trade rather profitable.

visual.cap: Table I · The one-carat question · indicative dollars per stone
visual.note: The gap is the luxury argument; the gap is also the value argument Two products wearing one name. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/091

sections.h: The scoreboard reads 61

p.text: Whatever position a jeweler holds on the natural-versus-grown question, the American aisle has already voted, and it voted for the machine by a margin that would end most arguments.

sections.h: Arithmetic, not compromise

p.text: The economics underneath the number are brutal in one direction and liberating in the other. Lab-grown wholesale prices fell another 14-15% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. A premium one-carat lab-grown stone now retails between $800 and $1,200, with entry-level goods available for a few hundred dollars.

For a generation, as the analyst Sherry Smith writes in National Jeweler, that is balancing a ring against homeownership, inflation and student debt, the choice stops feeling like a compromise and starts feeling like arithmetic.

p.lead: Smith's larger argument is that the trade has framed the question wrong.
p.text: The market is not either/or, she contends, but bifurcated: lab-grown owns value and accessibility, natural diamonds own luxury and rarity, and a retailer's job is building an environment where both can thrive rather than treating one as the other's obituary.

She also names the uncomfortable truth behind the natural side's slide: the industry stopped telling its story, and today's engagement customer did not grow up with the campaigns that made the diamond a requirement in the first place.

sections.h: What comes after the vote

p.lead: The scoreboard does not settle where prices go next.
p.text: This desk reported last week that lab-grown wholesale has been finding a floor, with some categories firming for the first time in two years, even as retail prices keep drifting down.

And the natural market's own data offered a countercurrent: one-carat natural prices have stirred, and De Beers' Gen Z research, whatever its methodology, claims record American interest in diamonds generally. A 61% share of a growing category is not the same as a 61% share of a fixed pie.

hero.bars_cap: What a Brazilian stone pays at the border · percent duty

changed.text: Eastern time on July 23, Brazilian goods entering the United States pick up a new 25% tariff under Section 301 of the Trade Act, the result of a year-long administration investigation that found Brazilian policies unreasonable burdens on US commerce.

means.text: Dealers holding polished Brazilian inventory stateside just watched its replacement cost jump by a third, and Paraíba, already the most supply-starved stone in the colored market, now has a customs multiplier on top of its scarcity one. Expect landed prices to move within weeks, and expect the phrase 'pre-tariff goods' to start appearing in dealer offers.
It will occasionally even be true.

visual.cap: Table I · What a Brazilian stone pays at the border · percent duty
visual.note: Value added in Brazil is what the tariff taxes The border prices the lapidary, not the stone. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/092

sections.h: Midnight, July 23

p.text: Layered on the existing 10% Section 122 duty, the effective rate on most Brazilian jewelry goods becomes 35% overnight. For a trade that prices in single percentage points, it is the largest single repricing of a major gem source since the 2025 tariff rounds.

sections.h: The carve-outs are the strategy

p.lead: The carve-outs are where the strategy lives.
p.text: Rough gemstones under HTS codes 7103.10.20 and 7103.10.40 are exempt, as are precious metals in unwrought and semi-manufactured form: silver, gold, platinum, palladium and rhodium all pass free. What pays is everything Brazil adds value to at home: cut and polished stones, and finished jewelry.

Sara Yood of the Jewelers Vigilance Committee noted the metals exemptions are "pretty broad" and consistent with prior policy, while confirming the polished and finished categories enjoy no such relief.

p.lead: The arithmetic has a second act.
p.text: The current 10% Section 122 tariff expires July 24, and a separate 12.5% duty tied to the administration's forced-labor investigation, which surveyed 60 countries and found Brazil among 54 falling short on enforcement, is waiting in the wings. When that activates, the combined rate lands at 37.5%.
Importers are effectively being asked to plan around three different totals inside a single season.

sections.h: Paraíba gets a multiplier

p.lead: What this means at the counter depends on the stone.
p.text: Brazil is the world's dominant source of fine tourmaline, including Paraíba, and a major supplier of aquamarine, topaz, amethyst and citrine, with a cutting industry centered on Minas Gerais that has spent decades moving up the value chain.

The exemption structure now pushes directly against that: rough leaving Brazil for cutting in the US or Asia travels duty-free, while a stone finished by a Brazilian lapidary pays 35% at the American border. The tariff, whatever its intent, is a subsidy for cutting Brazilian stones anywhere except Brazil.

hero.bars_cap: Four of the twelve · principal stones
hero.n: 12 brooches, each convertible to a pendant

changed.text: Graff has taken the butterfly, its house motif since 1975, and pinned it to one of jewelry's oldest formats. The London house's new high-jewelry capsule comprises twelve brooches designed as jabot pins, the double-ended fasteners of the seventeenth century, each one convertible into a pendant.

means.text: The brooch has been declared dead more often than the mechanical watch, and it keeps returning for the same reason: it is the only jewel that does not need a body part to justify it. Graff betting twelve high-jewelry pieces on jabot pins is a statement that the top of the market wants objects with mechanics, history and a second life.
The trade should note which of the twelve sells first: if it is Eva, the Paraíba gradient, the color market's fever has officially reached the brooch tray.

visual.cap: Table I · Four of the twelve · principal stones
visual.note: Bars indicate the desk's read of stone-work complexity, not price The named butterflies, under the loupe. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/093

sections.h: A 1975 motif, re-pinned

p.text: The wings are mounted en tremblant, on tiny sprung mechanisms, so the butterflies flutter with the wearer's movement rather than sitting still under glass.

sections.h: The full register of stones

p.lead: The stone work runs the house's full register.
p.text: Tamara sets a marquise-cut emerald at the center of an Art Deco sunburst in white gold and diamonds. Freya borrows an archival dragonfly design and paves its wings in fancy-cut and pear-shaped yellow diamonds.

Eva, the painterly one, arcs a gradient of sapphires, emeralds, Paraíba tourmalines and diamonds across its span, an effect the house traces to Monet's garden canvases, with miniature butterflies scattered around the principal one for extra motion.
Lina works square-cut pink sapphires into an invisible setting, finishing the jabot tip with a marquise pink sapphire and a pavé butterfly.
Design director Anne-Eva Geffroy framed the collection simply: "there is something deeply poetic about the form of a butterfly". The poetry has structure under it.

The jabot format solves the brooch's oldest commercial problem, which is that modern wardrobes give it nowhere to sit; a pin that becomes a pendant is two objects for one price, and the tip ornament, a single butterfly, emblem or jewel at the pin's opposite end, lets the piece read differently on a lapel, a knit or a gown.

sections.h: The brooch revival has numbers

p.lead: The capsule lands in a brooch market that is quietly reviving.
p.text: Auction bidders have spent two seasons paying attention to convertible and mechanical jewels, the couture houses put monumental brooches on half the fall runways, and en tremblant work, a nineteenth-century specialty, has become shorthand for the kind of handwork machine settings cannot fake.
All twelve pieces are priced on request, which at Graff's level of stone sourcing is less coyness than honesty: no two Paraíba gradients cost the same.

hero.bars_cap: Three lots, one lesson · hammer results, dollars

changed.text: The auction market's most interesting move this season is happening below the trophy line. Bonhams reports record results from its spring watch sales, and the names doing the work are not the usual two. Piaget models doubled and in some cases tripled in value, and Cartier posted similarly steep gains from lower starting prices.

means.text: Piaget doubling at auction while a 1930s Rolex sells for the price of a new Tissot is the same lesson twice: the market has stopped buying brands and started buying eras. The seventies gold shaped watch is this cycle's winner, and the houses with deep archives there, Piaget and Cartier above all, are effectively sitting on unpriced inventory.
Dealers should check their safes for bamboo lugs before Bonhams checks them first.

visual.cap: Table I · Three lots, one lesson · hammer results, dollars
visual.note: The market buys eras, not age; seventies gold beats thirties history The shape of current taste. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/094

sections.h: Below the trophy line

p.text: The evidence lots tell the story compactly: an 18-carat gold Cartier 'Bamboo' Coussin from the 1970s brought $114,800 in New York in April, and a gold Piaget Polo Jumbo from around 1980 made $33,280 in an online sale.

sections.h: A structural change

p.text: Jonathan Darracott, Bonhams' global head of watches, reads the results as a structural change rather than a hot streak: "demand extends far beyond a handful of trophy watches".

The bidder pool has broadened past the Rolex-and-Patek axis that defined the last decade, with younger and more diverse collectors driving the growth, and dress watches, the category the sports-watch era left for dead, are selling alongside the steel classics. Neo-vintage, the house believes, stays strong from here.

p.lead: The counter-evidence lot is as instructive as the records.
p.text: A gold-plated Rolex Prince from around 1930, a genuine piece of the crown's history, sold online for $2,176.

The market is not paying for age or even for the name in isolation; it is paying for design language it currently wants, and right-now taste favors the shaped gold watch, the integrated seventies silhouette, the piece that photographs like jewelry. A Prince, for all its history, looks like a museum's idea of a watch.

sections.h: The middle of the pyramid

p.lead: The pattern matches what the wider tape has shown all month.
p.text: Rolex, Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet still tighten their grip on secondary-market value retention, certified pre-owned premiums are compressing, and the seven-figure trophy segment keeps setting records at Sotheby's and Phillips.

What Bonhams' spring adds is the middle of the pyramid: five-figure money moving into names that cost four figures three years ago. That is how collecting categories mature, from a leaderboard into a landscape.

changed.text: François-Henri Bennahmias, the man who ran Audemars Piguet through its Royal Oak supercycle, has confirmed what the trade whispered for two years. "The rumours were true - I was trying to buy De Bethune", he told WatchPro, adding that the negotiations failed for several reasons and consumed a great deal of time.

means.who: The most bullish fact in this story is the failed deal itself.
means.text: When the executive who scaled AP to four billion francs tries to buy your 500-piece atelier and cannot close, the asset is either overpriced or underloved by no one, and in watchmaking those are the same thing.

De Bethune's owners are holding, its auction results are climbing, and the last Résonance-era independent with this much in-house credibility that came properly to market rewrote the price book. Watch the starry dials; the smart money already is.

visual.note: Results consistently above estimate through 2026 A 500-piece brand priced like a future blue chip. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/095

sections.h: The parlor question, settled

p.text: The admission settles one of independent watchmaking's favorite parlor questions and opens a better one: why does everyone with money keep circling this particular 500-piece brand?

sections.h: Why everyone circles it

p.lead: De Bethune is the connoisseur's independent almost by design.
p.text: Founded in 2002 by master watchmaker Denis Flageollet and partners, the Sainte-Croix house produces fewer than 500 pieces a year and manufactures its own hairsprings in-house, a capability perhaps a half-dozen companies on earth share.

Its titanium bridges, blued-steel starry dials and floating lugs are among the most recognizable design signatures in modern horology, and the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève has decorated it repeatedly, from the Aiguille d'Or in 2011 to the Men's Complication prize in 2024.

The brand Bennahmias could not buy belongs to The 1916 Company, which inherited it through WatchBox's 2021 investment. The current structure gives it executive chairman Justin Reis and, as of this year, chief executive Antoine Pin, the former TAG Heuer and Bulgari watch boss who replaced long-serving CEO Pierre Jacques.
It is a heavyweight management bench for a company whose annual output would fit in one modest shipping crate, which tells you what the owners believe the name is worth.

sections.h: The tape agrees

p.lead: The secondary market is making the same argument in numbers.
p.text: Recent auction results for the DB25 Starry Varius have ranged from roughly $42,000 to $135,500, consistently above estimate, and the brand's auction record stands at $190,500 for a 2018 DB28 Kind of Blue Tourbillon, set in 2023.

For a maker with barely two decades of history and microscopic production, that is the profile of a future blue chip, and investors who watched F.P. Journe values multiply tenfold have learned to move early.

hero.bars_cap: June by market · CHF millions

changed.text: The number the trade circled on its calendar arrived Tuesday, and it was better than almost anyone had penciled in. Swiss watch exports rose 11.2% in June to CHF 2.4 billion, the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry reported, on 1.3 million timepieces — volume up 11.7%, running slightly ahead of value.

means.text: Volume up 11.7% against value up 11.2% means this is a real recovery in units, not a mix trick — Switzerland sold more watches, not merely dearer ones. The France number deserves suspicion and attention in equal measure; doublings of that size usually say as much about logistics and tourist flows as about French wrists.
One good month is a data point. Two would be a direction.

visual.cap: Table I · June by market · CHF millions
visual.note: The top six markets took 53% of everything Switzerland shipped in June The federation's June table, largest markets. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/079

sections.h: The month arrives

p.text: After April's 16.6% drop and May's barely-there 0.4% gain, June is the first month of 2026 that reads like growth rather than stabilization, and it lands three days after a week in which the industry's news was mostly about who might buy whom.

sections.h: France doubles; America compounds

p.lead: The geography of the rebound is the story inside the story.
p.text: The United States, the industry's largest market, took CHF 349 million of watches in June, up 12.7% — steady, broad, and consistent with the American strength Richemont reported for its own quarter last week.

Britain added 12.2% to CHF 175 million, Japan 8.8%, Hong Kong 6.9%, Singapore 6.7%. And then there is France: CHF 250 million, up 103.5% — a doubling that vaulted it to second place among all markets and dragged the top six to 53% of everything Switzerland shipped.

sections.h: The barbell is official

p.lead: Price bands tell the sharper truth.
p.text: Watches priced between CHF 200 and 500 at export grew 54.1%, the entry segment under CHF 200 rose 9.9%, and pieces above CHF 3,000 gained 14.2%. The middle — CHF 500 to 3,000, the traditional home of the aspirational Swiss watch — fell 4.7%.

The barbell that retailers have described all year is now printed in the federation's own table: the customer is either buying an affordable Swiss name or a serious one, and the segment in between keeps paying for the clarity.

p.lead: One month does not repair a half.
p.text: January through June exports total CHF 12.8 billion, still 0.7% below last year, and the federation's spring was ugly enough that June's double-digit print only pulls the year back toward flat.

But direction matters in an industry that plans in decades, and the June table rhymes with everything else on this week's tape — Richemont's jewelry-led quarter, Watches of Switzerland's American year, and an auction market paying records for the top of the pyramid while the middle waits.

sections.h: The number lands

p.text: In July the board rebuffed takeover interest that valued the group around £1.75 billion, and Reuters had earlier reported talks with more than one potential bidder. A profit line up three-quarters is the kind of answer a board hopes to give after saying no.

sections.h: The circling resumes

p.text: The result did not end the conversation; by IDEX's account it restarted it.

The report notes fresh speculation about acquisition interest from both private equity and strategic buyers — unsurprising for a Rolex-anchored retailer that now earns the majority of its revenue in the United States, the one large market where June's export table showed steady double-digit growth.

p.lead: The backdrop makes the print more striking, not less.
p.text: The federation's own June data shows the CHF 500–3,000 export band — the middle of the market — down 4.7%, while pieces above CHF 3,000 grew 14.2%. Watches of Switzerland lives almost entirely on the right side of that divide.
When the market splits into a barbell, the company holding the authorized-dealer keys to the heavy end collects the difference, and 76% profit growth is what collecting it looks like.

sections.h: Arithmetic, then appetite

p.text: What happens next is arithmetic as much as appetite.

An approach at £1.75 billion was made against last year's earnings; any renewed bid now negotiates against this year's, plus a demonstrated willingness to say no. For the rest of the trade, the signal is simpler — the strongest balance sheets in watch retail are being built in American malls and London arcades, not in the middle of the price list.

hero.bars_cap: Rio Tinto's diamond wind-down · carats, millions

changed.text: The last chapter of Rio Tinto's diamond business is being written in leftovers.

means.text: Majors do not keep exploration teams in Angola out of nostalgia — Rio Tinto is leaving the mine, not the idea of diamonds. The industry should read the 33,000 carats accordingly: an ending, with a bookmark in it.

visual.cap: Table I · Rio Tinto's diamond wind-down · carats, millions
visual.note: From a producing mine to a closing entry in three reporting periods Diavik output, Rio Tinto Q2 operations review. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/081

sections.h: Leftovers, by the ton

p.text: The company's second-quarter operations review, reported by Rapaport on Monday, shows 33,000 carats recovered at Diavik between April and June — not from mining, which ended when the Northwest Territories operation reached the close of its life in March, but from processing the ore that remained on surface.
Output fell 97% from both the prior quarter and the year before, the arithmetic of a mine that no longer exists.

For the half, Diavik produced 1.1 million carats, down 51% from the first six months of 2025. Rio Tinto says it will continue to process and sell its final production through the end of 2026, which gives the market roughly five more months of Canadian goods carrying the Diavik name before the tap closes entirely.

sections.h: An arc closes

p.lead: The exit completes an arc two decades long.
p.text: Argyle in Australia — once the world's largest producer by volume and the source of nearly all its pink diamonds — closed in 2020. The stake in Fort à la Corne in Saskatchewan was sold in 2023.

Diavik was the last diamond asset on the books of a company that has decided its future is copper, iron ore and lithium. One wrinkle survives the funeral: Rio Tinto is keeping diamond exploration alive in Angola, the same ground where De Beers and Endiama have been mapping new kimberlites.

sections.h: Three names subtract at once

p.text: The supply math thickens a story this page has been tracking all month. Burgundy's Ekati went dark in June; Diavik is now processing its own remnants; De Beers has paused Venetia's underground for two years.

Three of the industry's storied names are subtracting carats at once, into a rough market that De Beers just repriced downward — a reminder that supply discipline is arriving the hard way, by exhaustion rather than by choice.

hero.bars_cap: Who the pause touches · positions in consultation

changed.text: The two-year pause at Venetia now has a payroll attached.

means.text: A two-year pause is a forecast wearing overalls — it says management believes rough prices will not recover before 2028. If the union extracts real alternatives to dismissal, the new owners will be glad someone did the fighting before they arrived.

visual.cap: Table I · Who the pause touches · positions in consultation
visual.note: South Africa's flagship diamond asset, idled while its owner is sold NUM figures for the Section 189A consultation. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/082

sections.h: The payroll gets a number

p.text: The National Union of Mineworkers said this weekend that De Beers' decision to halt production at South Africa's largest diamond mine places 1,214 workers into formal retrenchment consultation — 1,134 permanent employees at the Limpopo operation itself and a further 80 at De Beers Sightholder Sales South Africa, the company's Kimberley-based sales arm.
The process runs under Section 189A of the Labour Relations Act, the statutory large-scale consultation that obliges the company to consider alternatives before any dismissal.

sections.h: The union's terms

p.lead: The union's language was not conciliatory.
p.text: "Workers cannot be treated as disposable tools," said Masibulele Naki, the NUM's chief negotiator for the diamond sector, arguing that De Beers has understood the diamond market's deterioration for years and should have planned for its people accordingly.
The union wants the consultation to examine executive and management costs, retraining and upskilling programs, and cuts to non-essential spending before a single underground job is shed.

De Beers announced the Venetia pause this month as a cash-preservation measure — Bloomberg reported the plan on July 13 — after cutting rough prices at its July sight for a shrinking roster of buyers.

Venetia, which transitioned from open pit to underground mining at a cost of roughly $2 billion, was designed to anchor South African production into the 2040s. Idling it for two years mothballs the country's flagship diamond asset while the rough market works through its worst stretch in a generation.

sections.h: A sale in the background

p.lead: The consultation lands at the most awkward possible moment for the seller.
p.text: Anglo American has named the Gareth Penny-led consortium its preferred bidder for De Beers, and Botswana is still weighing how to exercise the freedom it says it has over its own 15%.
Whoever ends up owning the company inherits the outcome of the Section 189A process — and the labor relationships it either preserves or burns.

hero.bars_cap: Growth, by engine · percent, H1 2026

changed.text: American jewelry retail just printed a strong half built on a narrow base. Revenue rose 8.6% in the first six months of 2026 against the same period last year, according to retail analytics firm Tenoris, and June alone grew 13% — acceleration, not fade, into the summer.

means.text: An 8.6% half that rides a 19% ticket is thinner than it looks — revenue is up because each customer spends more, not because there are more customers. The number to watch into the holidays is the one nobody prints in a headline: how many boxes actually leave the store.

visual.cap: Table I · Growth, by engine · percent, H1 2026
visual.note: Price is growing more than twice as fast as revenue — units make up the difference, downward Tenoris retail panel, H1 2026. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/084

sections.h: A strong half, narrowly built

p.text: The engine, though, is price: the average purchase rose 19% across the half and 20% in June, while the number of items sold kept falling.

sections.h: Where the units went

p.lead: The unit decline is concentrated where most customers live.
p.text: Pieces priced under $1,500 — the bulk of American jewelry transactions — continue to shrink in unit terms, which means the growth is being carried by fewer, wealthier purchases.

Tenoris notes the shift favors specialty jewelers who lean into premium merchandise; it is harder news for anyone whose business is built on volume at the entry price points, where gold at $4,000 an ounce has quietly repriced the starter category out of its own customers' budgets.

By category, bracelets were the half's best performer, up 14% with double-digit growth in spend per item. Pendants and earrings grew more slowly but held solid; pearl jewelry, in Tenoris's telling, was a quiet standout — a thread this paper pulls separately today on the Gemstones desk.

sections.h: Two diamond machines

p.lead: The diamond counter split into two machines running opposite programs.
p.text: Natural diamond jewelry managed single-digit revenue growth on declining units and rising average prices — fewer stones, dearer stones.

Lab-grown diamond jewelry posted double-digit revenue growth driven by unit gains rather than price, the category still converting new customers even as its per-carat values sit near their floor. Same showcase, two different businesses.

hero.src: The June quarter in Greater China

changed.text: Hong Kong's jewelry chains just reported the kind of quarter that makes a strange market look simple: sell gold, and sell it where the tax is lower.

means.text: The gold counter is eating the diamond counter's lunch in Greater China, and the mainland's −58% diamond print is the loudest number on this week's tape. Until the diamond case earns back its investment story, the region's jewelers will keep being gold dealers with very good lighting.

visual.cap: Table I · Same-store sales, June quarter · Luk Fook, percent
visual.note: Diamonds ran the other way: −17% group, −58% on the mainland Luk Fook quarterly update, per Rapaport. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/085

sections.h: Two chains, one quarter

p.text: Luk Fook's retail sales value rose 32% in the quarter ended June 30, Rapaport reported, with group same-store sales up 39% — split between a 41% surge in Hong Kong and Macau and a 16% rise on the mainland.
Chow Sang Sang, reporting the same week, posted a 16% gain in quarterly retail value, with same-store sales up 30% in Hong Kong and Macau and 17% in mainland China.

sections.h: Gold 50, diamonds minus 17

p.text: The product mix behind those numbers is lopsided to the point of caricature. Luk Fook's gold product same-store sales rose 50% — 55% in Hong Kong and Macau, 21% on the mainland — as consumers kept treating the metal as an investment despite a volatile tape.

p.lead: Same-store diamond sales fell 17% group-wide, and collapsed 58% in mainland China.
p.text: Chow Sang Sang described gold demand as steady through the price swings, leaning on its signature collections.

p.lead: Policy is doing some of the pushing.
p.text: A new value-added tax treatment on the mainland widened the price gap between mainland counters and Hong Kong's, and customers responded the way arbitrage always responds: by getting on a train.
The border cities are collecting the difference — one more reason Hong Kong and Macau same-store growth is running at more than double the mainland's at both chains.

sections.h: Fewer doors, more sales

p.lead: Both retailers are shrinking their way to these numbers.
p.text: Luk Fook closed a net 148 shops in the quarter to stand at 2,857 worldwide; Chow Sang Sang has closed a net 49 this year and operates 776, with management prioritizing store productivity and prime locations.
More sales through fewer doors is the strategy on both sides — the physical network consolidating around the customers who still show up, checkbook in hand, for gold.

hero.bars_cap: The pearl ladder at Bonhams · pounds sterling

changed.text: Two very different ledgers agreed about pearls this month.

means.text: In a half defined by fewer boxes at higher prices, the category quietly adding buyers deserves more counter space than it is getting. The trade spent a decade calling pearls your grandmother's gem; the numbers now say the grandmother was early.

visual.cap: Table I · The pearl ladder at Bonhams · pounds sterling
visual.note: The distance between estimate and hammer is the market repricing scarcity Bonhams London jewels sale, July 8, per JCK. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/086

sections.h: Two ledgers agree

p.text: In Tenoris's first-half review of American jewelry retail — a half in which overall unit sales fell and growth leaned on ever-higher tickets — pearl jewelry stood out as a surprising strength, a category posting a solid run without the benefit of a bridal occasion or a metals tape to drive it.
Days earlier, the auction market had said the same thing with a hammer.

sections.h: The hammer confirms

p.text: At Bonhams' London jewels sale on July 8, a two-row natural pearl necklace with a diamond clasp brought £39,680, roughly $53,250, against an estimate of £10,000 — four times the low expectation. A David Morris cultured pearl and diamond necklace made £40,960 over a £25,000–35,000 estimate.

"Natural pearls, colored gemstones, signed, and period jewelry all performed strongly," said Jennifer Tonkin, Bonhams' head of jewelry in the UK, in JCK's account of the sale — results this page reported at the time, now looking less like one good afternoon and more like a pattern.

sections.h: A ladder customers can climb

p.lead: The design desks got there first.
p.text: Roseate's new Odyssey collection — pearls carrying luminous, hope-laden motifs, covered admiringly by the trade press this month — is one of a string of launches treating the pearl as a first-choice gem rather than an heirloom afterthought.

The category's case writes itself in 2026: an organic gem with no per-ounce tape attached, priced below the gold-and-diamond arms race, with a supply story at the natural end that auction results keep validating.

p.lead: There is a hierarchy inside the win.
p.text: Cultured goods are carrying the retail volume; natural pearls, finite by definition, are carrying the records.
The space between those two prices — a few hundred dollars to fifty thousand — gives the pearl something almost nothing else in the showcase has right now: a ladder a customer can actually climb.

sections.h: The save at $3,959

p.text: After the worst week in six left spot gold at levels last seen in November, Friday's session staged a late defense: the metal closed at $4,017.30, up $42.10 on the day, after trading as low as $3,959.30 — within five dollars of the triple bottom at $3,964 that technicians have watched all month.

p.lead: Monday's early tape confirmed the save rather than extending it.
p.text: At 5:45 a.m. ET, Kitco quoted spot at $4,018.20, up two cents, the week's first test already posted and passed.

sections.h: Oil argues with the Fed

p.lead: The tug-of-war that produced Friday's whipsaw has not gone anywhere.
p.text: On one side sits oil: Brent crude at $90.40 and WTI at $84.39, as strikes on Iran keep tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted and feed exactly the inflation arithmetic that hurts bullion by way of the Federal Reserve.

On the other side sits the rate market's answer — December hike odds near 82% in futures pricing, up from 73% at Friday's close, September readings near 60%, and the 30-year Treasury yield above 5%. Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack has argued for keeping rates higher for longer; the market has largely stopped arguing back.

p.lead: The technical map is unusually legible.
p.text: Below the market: $3,964, the triple bottom, then $3,886. Above it: the descending trendline near $4,025 that capped Monday's early attempt, the 50-period moving average at $4,045, then open air toward $4,093–$4,138 if that gives way.

Kitco's weekly survey caught Wall Street analysts leaning bearish for the near term while retail respondents split down the middle — and Bank of America, for its part, told clients to buy the dip and average down.

sections.h: Silver does the work

p.lead: The rest of the tape leaned the other way.
p.text: Silver did the complex's actual work Monday morning, up 1.67% at $56.76 after ending Friday at $55.83; palladium added 1.46% to $1,248 and platinum 0.38% to $1,596.

The calendar between here and the Fed's July 28–29 meeting is light but pointed: leading indicators Monday, jobless claims Thursday, PMIs and new-home sales Friday. Each print now reads as a vote on whether December's hike arrives — and each vote moves the metal the bench prices its work in.

changed.text: The world's cutting floor is moving again.

means.text: Value has come back before price, and work has come back before margin. An 8.7% rise built on $682 carats means the factories are busy again and the profit still isn't — but every diamond recovery in memory has started at exactly this end of the goods ledger.

sections.h: The factory moves again

p.text: India's gross gems and jewellery exports reached $2,212.6 million in June, up 26.5% from a year earlier, according to Gem & Jewellery Export Promotion Council data reported this past week — the sector's sharpest monthly gain in recent memory, landing after two years in which the trade's biggest factory mostly learned to shrink.

sections.h: Gold carries, diamonds turn

p.lead: The composition matters as much as the headline.
p.text: Gold jewellery carried the month, up 54.5% to $1,087.7 million — a number inflated by bullion itself, with gold roughly a fifth more expensive than a year ago, but too large to be price alone.

The quieter figure is the important one: cut-and-polished diamond exports rose 8.7% to $846.7 million, the category's first clean monthly increase after a slump that has closed mines on other continents.

p.lead: The quarter tempers the celebration.
p.text: April-through-June exports totalled $6,612.2 million, up just 0.04% — flat, in plain language. Cut-and-polished shipments for the quarter were $2,720.2 million, down 4.1% by value even as volume rose 8.9% to 3.98 million carats.
The average export price works out to $681.70 a carat: smaller and cheaper goods are doing the recovering, which squares with the small-stone turn this desk has been tracking since June.

sections.h: The quarter keeps it honest

p.lead: Upstream, the discipline holds.
p.text: Rough imports for the quarter fell 32.4% by value and 8.6% by volume to 6.69 million carats — Surat is still working down inventory rather than restocking on faith.
June's gross imports of $1,720.6 million, up 10.06%, suggest the restocking has at least begun, timed to a July De Beers sight where rough pricing was expected to ease.

changed.text: The preferred bidder was named in London; the answer came from Gaborone.

means.who: Anglo has chosen its buyer, but Botswana gets to choose the deal.
means.text: A pre-emption right held by a seller's most important partner is the closest thing M&A has to a veto, and Gaborone has now said, politely and in parliament, that it knows it.

visual.cap: Table I · What rides on the answer · percent

sections.h: Gaborone holds the cards

p.text: On Friday, Moeti Mohwasa, Botswana's minister for state president, defence and security, confirmed to lawmakers that Anglo American has selected the Global Diamond Consortium as preferred bidder for its 85% of De Beers — and then spent the rest of his statement reminding the room who actually holds the cards.

Botswana's 15% stake carries a right of first refusal, and Mohwasa said the state retains "complete freedom" in how it plays it: join the consortium as a partner, exercise pre-emption on its own, or exercise it alongside a third party of its choosing.
Nothing, in other words, has been decided except the identity of the party Botswana will be negotiating with — or against.

sections.h: A reunion at the table

p.lead: The consortium itself is a reunion.
p.text: It is led by Gareth Penny, De Beers' chief executive from 2006 to 2010 and now chair of asset manager Ninety One, with a Qatari investment fund and Israeli businessman Nir Livnat alongside; its proposal contemplates participation by Angola and Namibia.

The field has narrowed from six bidders in 2025 to two, and Anglo — which put De Beers up for sale in May 2024 — is aiming to close by the fourth quarter, subject to conditions that prominently include Botswana's approval.

sections.h: A nation, not a company

p.lead: The stakes in Gaborone are not corporate but national.
p.text: Diamonds account for roughly 80% of Botswana's exports and about a third of state revenue, and President Duma Boko's government has said openly that it wants a larger — even controlling — position in the company that sells them.
Every path to closing runs through the same capital city that just declined to commit itself.

hero.bars_cap: Net CO2 absorbed · thousand tonnes

changed.text: The greenest certificate in diamond mining now belongs to a company half the market is forbidden to buy from.

means.text: Sanctions are a political judgment and carbon is an atmospheric one, and the two do not cancel. Alrosa's certificate will not move a single stone through Antwerp — but it will be quoted in every Mumbai and Dubai showroom that stocks Russian goods, and the Western trade should have an answer ready.

visual.cap: Table I · Net CO2 absorbed · thousand tonnes
visual.note: Kimberlite weathers, gas replaces oil, and the ledger flips further negative Alrosa's stated net carbon absorption, per TÜV Austria verification. Carat Capital graphics desk.  CC/2026/074

sections.h: A certificate with an asterisk

p.text: TÜV Austria Standards & Compliance has verified Alrosa's operations and its entire 2025 production — 29.8 million carats — as carbon-neutral, the second consecutive year the Russian miner has earned the designation, the company said last week.

sections.h: The engineering is real

p.text: The engineering behind the number is real.

Alrosa completed the gasification of its Udachny division in 2025, moving it off petroleum fuels; 76% of its electricity now comes from renewable sources; and the kimberlite it processes absorbs carbon dioxide as it weathers, a quirk of diamond-bearing ore that the company counts on its side of the ledger.

Its facilities absorbed 126,000 tonnes more CO2 than they emitted last year, up from 37,000 tonnes in 2024, and its footprint per carat improved 60% to minus 1.18 kilograms of CO2 equivalent. Chief executive Pavel Marinychev says no other miner has certified both product and operations.

sections.h: The audience is selective

p.lead: The audience for the certificate is necessarily selective.
p.text: G7 import restrictions on Russian diamonds, phased in from 2024, keep Alrosa's rough out of American and European pipelines regardless of its carbon math.
The document speaks instead to India, China and the Gulf — the markets that now clear most Russian goods, and where sustainability language increasingly features in trade marketing.

p.lead: For the wider industry the optics are awkward.
p.text: Natural diamond marketing leans hard on provenance and planet, usually with the implication that virtue and Western supply chains travel together.

The loudest environmental credential in the mining half of the business now sits with the producer those supply chains excluded — a fact that complicates the pitch for everyone selling 'responsibly sourced' as a bundled promise.
